full_judgment:
Obaidul Hassan, J: The delay in filing the Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal No.1465- 1470 of 2012 is hereby condoned.
2. The Civil Appeal along with all Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal are disposed of by this common judgment as all of those involve common questions of law and similar facts.
Civil Appeal No.179 of 2011:
3. This appeal by leave is filed against the judgment and order dated 13-12-2009 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.1424 of 2009 making the Rule absolute.
4. One Sinku Akramuzzaman writ petitioner-respondent filed the Writ Petition being No.1424 of 2009 impugning a notification being No.Shakha-10/1-Moti-88/82/344 dated 18-11-2007 (Annexure-H to the Writ Petition) published in the Bangladesh Gazette dated 7-2-2008 amending earlier Gazette dated 23-9-1986 whereby plot No.5/7, Bangabandhu Avenue, Dhaka has been corrected to read as plot No.7, Bangabandhu Avenue, Dhaka and thereby declared plot No.7 as abandoned property.
5. The respondent filed the writ petition contending, inter alia, that he is a shareholder Director and Chairman of Dienfa Limited, a Public Limited Company, incorporated in the erstwhile East Pakistan having its registered office at Ramna, Dhaka in Bangladesh. The shareholders of the Company were members of the Dhaka Nawab Family, who had landed properties around Bangabandhu Avenue and the said land was acquired by the erstwhile Government of East Bengal for creating a commercial area known as Nawbpur Shopping Area Extension, Dhaka. The then Government of East Bengal leased out for 99 years commencing from 21-1-1954 an area of 16.28 Kathas of land situated in Ward No.3, Dhaka Municipality under Lalbagh Police Station, Dhaka being plots No.48, 49.and 50 of Mouza/ Land No.TP /118/49 dated 14-11-1949 of the Consulting Architect, Government of East Bengal, C&B Department and allotted plots were subsequently numbered as holding No.7, Bangabandhu Avenue, by the Dhaka Municipality. The company obtained a loan of Taka 1,50,000 from the then Eastern Federal Union Insurance Company Ltd. by mortgaging the said land and constructed a multi-storied commercial building known as Dienfa Building and thereafter leased out most of the spaces to the said Eastern Federal Union Insurance Company Limited for its office in Dhaka. The loan was duly repaid by Dienfa Limited while the said Eastern Federal Union Insurance Company Limited continued to occupy the 1st, 2nd and 3rd floors of the said Dienfa Limited on monthly rental basis. After liberation of Bangladesh the Eastern Federal Union Insurance Company Ltd. became Jibon Bima Corporation and its Officers started to pretend that the Building of 7, Bangabandhu Avenue became a property of Jibon Bima Corporation. The writ-respondent No.3, Jibon Bima Corporation took lease of further spaces from the company as a tenant and the rest of the spaces of the ground floor and part of the 1st floor were rented out by the Company to different firms for commercial purposes on a monthly rental basis.
6. After liberation of Bangladesh the Company continued to be a Bangladeshi Company having submitted statement of accounts and other statutory documents to the Registrar, Joint Stock Companies, Bangladesh. Because of the death of most of the shareholders of the Nawab Family the secretarial function of the company could not be performed on regular basis. Three major shareholders of the company, namely, Khawja Sadderuddin, his wife Mrs. Chandi Sadderuddin and his sister Julekha Morshed, wife of late KG Morshed died and their shares were claimed by their heirs and accordingly an application was filed by the said heirs before the High Court Division in Matter No. 8 of 1989 for rectification of Share Register under section 38 of the Companies Act. The application was allowed by the High Court Division by the judgment and order dated 11-2-1990 allowing the rectification and directing the company to rectify the Register accordingly. The building at 7, Bangabandhu Avenue owned by Dienfa Limited was not rightly included in the 'Ka' list of notification dated 23-9-1986 published in the Gazette Extraordinary as the said building was never in possession of the government. The said notification included holding No.5/7, Bangabandhu Avenue, Dhaka which had been in possession of the government and the office of the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh (TCB) was in the said plot and at the ground floor there were other shops. The Government of Bangladesh published supplementary list of the abandoned properties of Bangladesh from time to time. But the Government with a mala fide motive included the plot No.7 through amendment as abandoned property by the impugned Gazette Notification (Annexure-H to the Writ Petition). Assailing the said Gazette the respondent filed writ petition and a Rule was issued.
7. The writ-respondent No.1-appellant No.1 contested the Rule by filing Affidavit-in-Opposition controverting the material facts stated in the writ petition contending, inter alia, that the writ petitioner has no locus standi to move the petition as he has not been an aggrieved person by the impugned Notification, despite the Nawab Family was the owner of the premises, they did not file any case for rectification of the holding No.7 and, as such, the writ petition was not maintainable.
8. Upon hearing the parties the High Court Division made the Rule absolute by judgment and order dated 13-12-2009. Having been aggrieved with the aforesaid judgment and order dated 13-12-2009, the appellants preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1398 of 2010 before this Court and this Division was pleased to grant leave on 28-11-2010 to consider the following grounds:
(I) Whether, the writ petitioners produced the title documents in respect of the case property and whether their claim in respect of the case property is maintainable and whether the High Court Division considered that the writ petition is maintainable or not.
(II) Whether, section 21 of the General Clauses Act empowered the Government to make correction of its order and accordingly the Government having exercised its power has corrected the entire Gazette Notification in respect of the Abandoned Properties and whether the writ petitioner annexed necessary papers to established their ownerships in respect of the case property and the High Court Division committed error in declaring the action of the Government illegal.
(III) Whether, the writ-petitioner claimed that the case property belongs to a limited company and there being any statement in the writ petition that all the share holders of the said company were present in Bangladesh at the time of promulgation of PO 16 of 1972 and whether the said limited company claimed the property in question, the instant writ petition filed by an alleged transferee of a shareholder is not maintainable.
(IV) Whether, the facts and circumstances of the case clearly show that it involves the disputed question of facts as regards the ownership of the case property, the High Court Division committed an error in deciding the instant matter in writ jurisdiction.
Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal Nos.280 of 2010 and 1465 of 2012:
9. These Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal have arisen out of the judgment and order dated 13-12-2009 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.723 of 2009 making the Rule absolute.
10. One Shafiul Alam (Shajahan) filed the writ petition contending inter alia that he has been running the business of Shoe Retail Store and Hair Dressing under the name and style of Keya Shoes and Gulistan Hair Dresser at the shopping space measuring about 515 sft. located on the ground floor of plot No.7, Bangabandhu Avenue, which is popularly known as Dienfa building owned by Dienfa Limited. The said space was originally leased out with a right to transfer possession by Dienfa Limited to one Khorshed Pall, proprietor of AD Pall & Sons with effect from 9-12-1955, who was running a business of tailoring shop popularly known as AD Pall & Sons. Said Khorshed Pall was paying monthly rent to Dienfa Limited and subsequently he transferred his right of possession to MA Rashid, proprietor of new AD Pall & Sons and thus said MA Rashid became the tenant of Dienfa Limited. Thereafter, said MA Rashid transferred his possession to the writ petitioner. Having taken possession of the said space the writ petitioner has been paying rent at the rate of Taka 1,200 per month. But he became shocked and surprised to receive memos No. ব:বে:বি:/ঢাকা/৪৭৭০ and ব:বে:বি:/ঢাকা/৪৭৬৮ dated 23-11-2008 issued by the writ-respondent No.3, the Executive Engineer, PWD, Tejgaon demanding Taka 13,02,484 and Taka 6,12,609 respectively as arrear rent of the said space from 1-1-1972 to 30-11-2008. On query the writ petitioner came to know that the said property of plot No.7 had been enlisted as abandoned property by gazette dated 7-2-2008. Dienfa Limited is the owner of the said property, but the government illegally enlisted the same as abandoned property. The writ petitioner filed writ petition before the High Court Division challenging the memos dated 23-11-2008.
11. The High Court Division issued Rule and subsequently on 13-12-2009 upon hearing made the Rule absolute.
Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal Nos.1466- 1470 of 2012:
12. These Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal have arisen out of the judgment and order dated 14-12-2009 passed by the High court Division in Writ Petitions No.724-727 of 2009 and 735 of 2009 making all the Rules absolute.
13. Those writ petitions were filed by various persons contending inter alia that the property of plot No.7, Bangabandhu Avenue, Dhaka originally belonged to Dienfa Limited. They acquired the possession of various commercial spaces of the said building by way of some successive transfers to different persons from Dienfa Limited at different rate of rents and they 1 kad been possessing the same from the time of purchasing possession. But the writ petitioners became shocked and surprised to receive various memos dated 23-11-2008 issued by the writ respondent No.3, the Executive Engineer, PWD, Tejgaon demanding arrear rents of those space from 1-1-1972 to 30-11-2008. On query the writ petitioners came to know that the said property of plot No.7 had been enlisted as abandoned property by gazette dated 7-2-2008. Dienfa Limited is the owner of the said property and they have been paying rent to the company, but the government illegally enlisted the same as abandoned property. The writ petitioners filed Writ Petitions No.724, 725, 726, 727 and 735 of 2009 before the High Court Division challenging different memos dated 23-11-2008.
14. The High Court Division issued Rules and subsequently on 14-12-2009 upon hearing made all the Rules absolute.
15. Mr AM Amin Uddin, the learned Attorney-General along with Mr ABM Siddiqur Rahman, Advocate and Mr Sukumar Biswas, Advocate appearing for the appellants as well as for the petitioners in Civil Petitions have contended that the land of plot No.7 was taken lease by Dienfa Limited from the then Government of East Pakistan, but none of the directors nor the company secretary was present in the country in 1972. All of them left the country in 1971 and in their absence the property of plot No.7 became abandoned as per section 2(1) of the PO 16 of 1972, thus the Government of Bangladesh became the owner of the property on plot No.7, Bangabandhu Avenue. The learned Counsels have submitted next that the government enlisted the property as abandoned on 23-9-1986, but inadvertently plot No.5/7 was stated instead of plot No.7, whereas there is no existence of plot No.5/7 and the land of plot No.7 was possessed before 1972 by Dienfa Limited. To cure the said mistake the government made correction by way of amendment in the gazette by notification dated 18-11-2007 and the said amendment was done within the ambit of section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897. One Sinku Akteruzzaman fabricating some documents claimed to be major shareholders of Dienfa Limited and filed the Writ Petition No.1424 of 2009, but he has no locus standi to file the same. The learned Counsels argued next that the petitioners in Writ Petition Nos. 723, 724, 725, 726, 727 and 735 of 2009 have been claiming the interest in the property of suit plot by creating a series of documents by which they claimed to have acquired right of possession through some successive transfers from Dienfa Limited, on other hand, since no director of Dienfa Limited was present after 1971 the property of plot No.7 was enlisted as abandoned and, as such, the writ petitioners have not acquired any right in the suit plot. But the High Court Division without appreciating the facts and law illegally made all the Rules absolute. To buttress his submission the learned Attorney-General referred the decisions reported in 10 ADC 1 = 17 BLC (AD) 196; 42 DLR (AD) 245; 28 DLR (AD) 120; 30 DLR (AD) 101.
16. Per contra, Mr Kamal-ul-Alam, the learned Senior Counsel on behalf of the respondents made a good endeavour to curtail the arguments put forward by the learned Attorney-General. At the outset the learned Senior Counsel has submitted that the building and the land adjunct thereto of plot No.7 belonged to Dienfa Limited and on behalf of the company one Khwaja Sadderuddin used to manage and supervise the company, subsequently he went abroad after 28-2-1972 and due to his illness the Annual General Meeting could not be held for the years 1972-1989, but later on, the said delay was condoned in Matter No.27 of 1989 by the High Court Division. The learned Counsel has contended  next that although Khwaja Sadderuddin was staying abroad the company was under his management and the building of plot No.7 was possessed by the company, despite that the government most illegally enlisted the building as abandoned. The learned Counsel has submitted next that the office of Dienfa Limited is in the disputed building and some spaces of the building had been rented to Jiban Bima Corporation and some spaces had been rented to some other persons. But the government without considering the facts enlisted the building as abandoned property. The learned Counsel has argued further that according to the Ordinance, 1985 the government cannot enlist any property as abandoned after 31st October 1988, but the disputed property has been enlisted as abandoned on 18-11-2007. The learned Counsel has contended next that Sinku Akramuzzaman the writ petitioner-respondent in Civil Appeal No.179 of 2011 acquired majority share of Dienfa Limited by way of various legal instruments from the legal heirs of Khwaja Sadderuddin and he is also the Chairman of the company and, as such, he has locus standi to file Writ Petition No.1424 of 2009 challenging the enlistment of property as abandoned. The learned Counsel contended next that the respondents in all the Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal are the tenants of Dienfa Limited and they have been possessing different spaces of plot No.7 and paying rents to the company, but the government violating the legal provisions claimed arrear rents. The learned Counsel for the respondents lastly contended that the High Court Division has not committed any illegality in making all the Rules absolute. The learned Senior Counsel has bolstered his argument referring a plethora of judgments of both domestic and foreign jurisdictions.
17. For convenience, the Civil Appeal No.179 of 2011 is discussed first. At the threshold it divulges from the record that the core contention between the parties majorly revolves around three-fold questions. Firstly, whether the building appertaining to the land of plot No.7 can be treated as abandoned property or not. Secondly, whether the inclusion of the disputed plot No.7 instead of plot No.5/7 by way of amendment dated 18-11-2007 in the earlier Gazette dated 23-9-1986 comes within the mischief of section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897. Thirdly, whether the writ petitioner-respondent had locus standi to file the writ petition.
18. It is advantageous to learn how the term 'abandoned property' has been defined in the law of our country. The definition of 'abandoned' property has been given in Article 2(1) of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 (shortly PO No.16 of 1972) which runs as follows:
"2. In this Order, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context—
(1) "abandoned property" means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose where-abouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, including—
(i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh;
(ii) any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking, Over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 (Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972), but does not include-
(a) any property the owner of  which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh;
(b) any property which is in the possession or under the control of the Government under any law for the time being in force.
Explanation : "Person who is not present in Bangladesh" includes anybody of persons or company constituted or incorporated in the territory or under the laws of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh;"
19. Thus, as per Article 2(1) of the PO No.16 of 1972 abandoned property denotes property owned by a person who is either (i) not present in Bangladesh, or (ii) whose whereabouts are not known, or (iii) who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property. According to the settled proposition of law expounded by this Division in the case of Bangladesh vs ATJ Industries reported in 28 DLR (AD) 120; Bangladesh vs Speedbird Navigation Ltd., reported in 30 DLR (AD) 101 all the aforesaid three sub-clauses have been used disjunctively and there is no need to construe them conjunctively.
20. Admittedly, Dienfa Limited, a public limited company incorporated in the erstwhile East Pakistan and the shareholders of the company were members of the Dhaka Nawab family and the Government of East Bengal leased out the land of alleged plot for 99 years commencing from 21-1-1954 in favour of Dienfa Limited.
21. Now let us examine whether Dienfa Limited had ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person its property. It is no doubt that Dienfa Limited is a person too as per Explanation to Article 2 of the PO No.16 of 1972. The respondent annexed a petition of Matter No.27 of 1990 in the additional paper book. On going through the Matter No.27 of 1990 admitted on 16-8-1989 it appears that the same was filed under section 79(3) read with section 76 of the Companies Act, 1913 for condonation of delay in holding Annual General Meeting (AGM), It divulges from the record that on 8-11-1990 the High Court Division allowed the application for condonation and the company was permitted to hold its AGM for the years from 1972 to 1989 on or before 31st day of December, 1990. Paragraphs No.3, 5 and 9 of the said Matter are extracted in the following:
"3. That the father of the petitioner late Mr Khawja Sadderuddin was one of the founder directors and a major shareholder of the company in the year 1971 and also acting as its Secretary till his death on 26-5-1985 but he was ill since 1972 and had been living abroad and, as such, could not organize the company properly nor could he convene any Annual General Meeting after the last Annual General Meeting held in the year 1971.
5. That as late Khawja Sadderuddin was the single major shareholder of the company, he used to run the whole management of the company and on his death the company and its assets are completely in mismanagement and the petitioner although sole heir of late Khawja Sadderuddin could not deal with the properties of the company so long as they were not included as shareholders of the company by way of rectification of share register under due process of law.
9. That as already stated the last Annual General Meeting was held for the year 1971. Due to absence of Khawja Sadderuddin on account of illness for a long time out of the country, the Annual General Meeting could not be held. In the meantime Mrs. Zulaikha Morshed and another director also died and on their death the Annual General Meeting of the Company due in the year 1972 on wards could not be convened or held without rectification of the share register."
22. It is evident from the above that Khawja Sadderuddin, the single major shareholder of the company who used to run the company has been out of Bangladesh before the day of promulgation of the PO No.16 of 1972 and there was none from Dienfa Limited in the country from 1972 to 1989 to supervise or manage the property in question. Although the respondent tries to establish that Khawja Sadderuddin worked as Secretary to the company till 3-3-1972, but it does not create a conclusive presumption that Khawja Sadderuddin stayed in Bangladesh till 3-3-1972 rather it gives rise to a reasonable inference that he left the country before 1972 after holding the Annual General Meeting of the Company in 1971 and died on 26-5-1985 while staying abroad.
23. Apart from this, it is manifest from the record that Taki Sadderuddin from which the writ petitioner by a power of attorney claimed to have acquired share of the company, kept mysteriously silent about the whereabouts of his father Khawja Sadderuddin until the year 1989 when he approached the High Court Division in Matter No. 8 of 1989 and 27 of 1989 for rectification of share register and condonation of delay in holding the AGM of the Company i.e. Dienfa Limited. On going through the Matter No. 8 of 1989 it appears that all the fifteen petitioners in Matter No.08 of 1989 have been living abroad except three petitioners including Taki Sadderuddin, the son of late Khawja Saderuddin. However, the major shareholder and Manager of Dienfa Ltd. Khawja Saderuddin, from which the petitioners in the Matter No.08 of 1989 claimed shares as heirs, had left Bangladesh before 1972.
24. In the given circumstances, it is squarely found that the then Company Secretary, Khawja Sadderuddin left the country in the year 1971 and in his absence none of the directors was available in the country or any one on behalf of the company to take responsibility to supervise or manage the company i.e. Dienfa Lmited and, as such, the alleged building appertaining to plot No.7 although earlier owned by Dienfa Lmited, but subsequently after 1971 it has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person the said property. On the other hand, PO No.16 of 1972 came into effect on 28-2-1972. Admittedly, the writ petitioner-respondent is an alleged transferee of those shares. Thus, there is no doubt to say that the alleged buildings and the adjunct lands thereto was not under occupation or supervision or management by Dienfa Limited on 28-2-1972, thereby the alleged property has been legally treated as abandoned property under Article 2(1) of the PO No.16 of 1972.
<u>25. Section 5(1) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provision) Ordinance, 1985 (shortly the Ordinance, 1985) lays down that the government shall, after the commencement of the Ordinance and before the 31st day of December, 1988, publish, from time to time, in the official Gazette, lists of buildings the possession of which have been taken as abandoned property under the PO No.16 of 1972. Accordingly, the government by virtue of section 5(1) of the Ordinance, 1985 published the alleged property as an abandoned property in the Gazette Notification dated 23-9-1986 stating that the possession of which has been taken by the government as abandoned property. But the fact remains that, the plot number mentioned in the Gazette Notification dated 23-9-1986 was inadvertently mistaken. After coming the said matter to the notice, the government brought amendment on 18-11-2007 which was published in the Gazette dated 7-2-2008 to cure such inadvertent mistake. Further, according to section 5(2) of the Ordinance, 1985 the lists published under section 5(1) shall be conclusive evidence of their being abandoned property and have vested in the government. Therefore, the property is vested in the government by operation of law. However, Jibon Bima Corporation being a government instrumentality is in possession of the property under the control, supervision and management of the government. It is worth to mention here that the adjacent plot No.8, Bangabandhu Avenue, is also an abandoned property and is under possession of Jibon Bima Corporation. From the foregoing discussion it is evident that the alleged land of plot No.7 is an abandoned property.</u>
26. The learned Counsel on behalf of the respondents by referring the case of Khan Brothers vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR (AD) 423; M/s Helal Jute Press Ltd. vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR 551 and Gannysons Ltd. vs Sonali Bank reported in 37 DLR (AD) 42 has contended that the government cannot treat the alleged property due to absence of its secretary namely Khwaja Sadderuddin.
27. It appears from the facts of Khan Brothers vs Government of Bangladesh, reported in 27 DLR (AD) 423 that on 31-1-1972, QA Rashid was appointed Director-in-Charge of the Company instead of Khan A Sabur and the company was run by the Director-in-Charge, meaning thereby the property was under the management of the company. But in the present case since 1972 till now no one of the company has been in Bangladesh to manage or control or supervise the property in question, thus the ratio of the case of Khan Brothers has no manner of application in the present case and therefore the declaration of the property in question as abandoned one is valid under PO No.16 of 1972.
28. Similarly, in the case of M/s Helal Jute Press Ltd. vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR 551, one of the directors has been in Bangladesh throughout and managing director was temporarily outside Bangladesh, but in a friendly country, India and the property of the company was not declared abandoned by the Court. However, in the instant case, not only Mr Khawja Sadderuddin, but all the members and shareholders of the company at the relevant time i.e., after holding the AGM in 1971-till 28-2-1972, had not been in Bangladesh. Therefore, it is apparent that the fact of the present case is distinguished from of the case referred to the writ petitioner-respondent.
29. In the case of Gannysons Ltd. vs Sonali Bank reported in 37 DLR (AD) 42 the directors of Gannysons Ltd. have always been in Bangladesh and even those who were temporarily outside the country returned to Bangladesh long ago. In the present case, no directors of the company were in Bangladesh since 1972. However, new directors came into scene after rectification of share register and purported transfer of shares which itself is questionable.
30. This Division observed in the case of the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary vs Orex Network Limited and others reported in 10 ADC 1 = 17 BLC (AD) 196 that once a property is enlisted by government as abandoned one has nothing to deny claims of claimants nor disclose the basis of treating it as abandoned property. Referring the previous decisions rendered by this Division it has been observed in paragraphs No.21, 22 and 24 which is extracted as follows:
"21. In the case of Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works vs Md Jalil and others reported in 48 DLR (AD) 10, this Division held as under:
The anus, therefore, is squarely on the claimant of the building to prove that the building is not an abandoned property. The Government has no obligation either to deny the facts alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property merely because the same is disputed by the claimant.
22. Reliance may be made in the case of the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works vs KM Zaker Hossain and others 8 BLC (AD) 27, it has been held as under:
18. Since the property has been listed under section 5(1) of the Ordinance as abandoned property and the said list has been published in the official Gazette, the claimant to the property i.e. respondent No. 1 was required to dislodge statutory presumption as under section 5(2) of the Ordinance that the property in question was not an abandoned property and that the same has been wrongly listed as abandoned property.
24. In the case of Hazerullah vs Chairman, 1st Court of Settlement and another reported in 3 BLC (AD) 42, it has been held that onus lies upon the claimants of the building to prove that the building is not an abandoned property and that the appellant having failed to discharge such onus the High Court Division rightly upheld the order of inclusion of the disputed property in the list of abandoned buildings."
31. In the conspectus of the decisions mentioned above, we find that although the onus was on the writ petitioner-respondent but he has pitiably failed to prove that the disputed property was illegally enlisted as abandoned property.
32. It transpires from the Memorandum and Articles of Association of Dienfa Limited that at the time of incorporation of the company the issued shares were 2,336, amongst them Khawja Sadderuddin had 317 shares. In the petition of Matter No.8 of 1989 filed under section 38 of the Companies Act, 1913 for rectification of share register it is mentioned that Khawja Sadderuddin died on 26-5-1985 and he had 3,550 shares out of 16,680 ordinary shares of Taka 10 each and said Khawja Sadder-uddin had been the founder director and main functionary of the company. Taki Saderuddin being the son of Khawja Sadderuddin and being constituent attorney of fourteen other petitioners majority of whom lived abroad filed the case. However, whether the Power of Attorneys are legally executed, authenticated and validated in Bangladesh remains a legal question and creates serious doubt about their validity. These Power of Attorneys are not valid documents in the eye of law. The shares of Khawja Sadderuddin had been rectified pursuant to the judgment in Matter No.8 of 1989. Since the judgment had been obtained by fraudulent Power of Attorneys, that judgment also lost its force in law and all subsequent actions are null and void.
33. It emerges from the record that writ petitioner-respondent claimed to have acquired the shares of the company belonging to, amongst others, the heirs of Khawja Sadderuddin by way of transfer. All the heirs of Khawja Sadderuddin including Taki Sadderuddin executed Power of Attorneys in favour of Khawja Shamsuddin from abroad including Pakistan and the said Khawja Shamsuddin has been abroad as well whose address was 1710, 137 place SE Bellevue Washington No.8005, United States of America. All those Power of Attorneys are not validly executed and authenticated tinder the Evidence Act read with section 18 of the Stamp Act. Being empowered by those so-called Powers of Attorneys Khawja Shamsuddin transferred the shares to the writ petitioner on 10-8-2004. It further appears from the record that Khawja Shamsuddin has been living in USA and the so-called aforesaid Power of Attorneys were executed in between 2003-2004 which seems to be after-thought and created to grab the disputed property and thus creates a serious doubt as to the genuineness of the whole transaction. In the aforesaid backdrop, all the Power of Attorneys by way of which the transfer of shares have been made are not valid Power of Attorneys and, as such, transfer of shares to the writ petitioner based on those invalid Power of Attorneys is also void and illegal which cannot create any legal right in favour of the writ petitioner to claim the property in question.
34. The learned Counsel for the respondent referring the case of Anath Bandhu & Sons Ltd. vs Balm Shudhanshu reported in 42 DLR (AD) 245 has argued that the Power of Attorneys executed outside of the country can still be cured by proper stamping. But the ratio decided in the said case is not applicable in the present case since the authentication had not been made and in the meantime the constituted attorney has become ficnctus officio.
<u>35. Further, the writ petitioner claiming himself as a shareholder director and chairman of Dienfa Limited, a public limited company filed the writ petition on his personal capacity as shareholder director not on behalf of the company. Under the law, only company being the juristic person can represent all shareholders of the company. Thus, it is palpably clear that the respondent has no locus standi to file the writ petition.</u>
<u>36. The very existence of Dienfa Limited is not also beyond question since the Certificate of Incorporation of the company shows that the same was issued on 29th April 1948 by the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies of East Pakistan. Factually, in 1948, there was no existence of East Pakistan, but officially it was East Bengal.</u>
37. Again, the writ petitioner-respondent could not establish his ownership or legal title of the property in question by producing any authentic or genuine title deeds, thus it is a disputed question of fact which cannot be decided in writ jurisdiction and, as such, the writ is not maintainable.
38. From the foregoing discussion, it is Unerringly clear that the writ petitioner-respondent had no locus standi to file the writ petition but the High Court Division most illegally made the Rule absolute.
39. Now we advert to a pertinent point as to whether the amendment of Gazette dated 23-9-1986 by subsequent gazette 7-2-2008 comes within the mischief of section 21 of the. General Clause Act, 1897. Section 21 of the General Clause Act lays down in the following:
"21. Where, by any Act of Parliament or Regulation, a power to issue notifications, orders, rules, or bye-laws is conferred, then that power includes a power, exercisable in the like manner and subject to the like sanction and conditions (if any), to add to,  amend, vary or rescind any notifications,  orders, rules or bye-laws so issued."
<u>40. It is apparent from the record that by a Gazette Notification dated 23-9-1986, the government declared plot Nos. 5/7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 15, 16/A, 18, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 30, 33 Sr 37 of Bangabandhu Avenue as abandoned property. However, mistakenly plot No.5/7 was printed instead of plot No.7. It is noted that there is no existence of any plot bearing No.5/7 at Bangabandhu Avenue which proves that it is a bona fide mistake of the government and the same has been corrected by notification dated 18-11-2007 published in the Gazette dated 7-2-2008. Moreover, plot Nos.7 and 8 both are being possessed by Jibon Bima Corporation, the instrumentality of the government. Apart from this, the Government by Gazette Notification dated 23-9-1986 also declared plot Nos. 5/A, 6, 12 and 6 of Bangabandhu Avenue as ‘Kha’ listed property at page No. 9764(6) of which the land of plot No.5/A, owned by the Ministry of Commerce, was sold out to the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh(TCB) on 14-12-1983  by a registered Deed. It, thus, leads to a logical conclusion that the government mistakenly printed plot No.5/7 instead of plot No.7 while publication of the Gazette which was subsequently amended on 18-11-2007 to cure the said mistake. It is not a declaration of new property as abandoned property rather correction of mistake which has already been declared as abandoned property by Gazette Notification dated 23-9-1986. Therefore, the said amendment of gazette invariably attracts the mischief of section 21 of the General Clause Act, 1897 and, as such, the government has not committed any illegality in treating the alleged land as abandoned property. But the High Court Division failing to appreciate the facts of the case as well as the provisions of law, most illegally held that the government treated the alleged property as abandoned property after 31st December, 1988 in violation of section 5 of the Ordinance, 1985.</u>
41. Relying on the case of Azizuddin Industries vs. Government of Pakistan reported in 18 DLR 92 and the case of Chief Controller of Imports and Exports vs Hussain Ali Shah A. Fazlani PLD reported in 1960 SC 310 The learned Counsel for the writ petitioner- respondent has contended that the power to add to, amend, vary or rescind under section 21 of the General Clauses Act, such power does not include the authority to take away a validly acquired right. Further, referring the case of Bangladesh vs Amena Khatun reported in 53 DLR (AD) 55 and Abdur Rashid Molla vs Bangladesh reported in 58 DLR (AD) 20 the learned Counsel of the respondent has also contended that since no notice was issued by the government to the writ petitioner-respondent as contemplated under Article 7 of PO No.16 of 1972 and section 5 of the Ordinance, 1985, the listing of the building as abandoned property is illegal. Regarding the aforesaid contention our view is that the aforesaid decisions have no manner of application in the case in hand inasmuch as in the case in hand the respondent could not prove that the disputed property was managed and possessed by Dienfa Limited on 28-2-1972 and, as such, the notice as contemplated in Article 7 of PO No.16 of 1972 and section 5 of the Ordinance, 1985 is not required in the present case. Further, by the amendment of gazette on 18-11-2007 there arises no question of taking away of a validly acquired right of Dienfa Limited or the writ petitioner since the disputed building had been enlisted as abandoned property on 23-9-1986.
42. Apart from the above mentioned cases the learned Counsel on behalf of the respondents referred to a plethora of judgments of Indian Supreme Court, but in the present context, those are not being discussed elaborately, because the ratio of those cases has no direct bearing in the cases in hand.
<u>43. At this juncture, we advert to the matters relating to Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal Nos. 280 of 2010, 1465-1470 of 2012. It appears that the High Court Division while disposing of the Writ Petition Nos. 723, 724, 725, 726, 727 and 735 of 2009 filed by the leave petitioners relied on the judgment and order dated 13-12-2009 passed in Writ Petition No.1424 of 2009 and observed that since the property of plot No.7, Bangabandhu Avenue, Dhaka was rightly possessed and owned by Dienfa Limited, the writ respondents committed illegality in enlisting the said plot as abandoned property. It has also been observed that the writ petitioners as transferee or tenants acquired the possession of various commercial spaces by way of several successive transfers from Dienfa Limited and, as such, they were not bound to pay rent to the government. In this regard, our considered view is that since from the foregoing discussion it is proved that the government rightly enlisted disputed property as abandoned and the same is under control and possession of the Government, the writ petitioners in Writ Petition Nos. 723, 724, 725, 726, 727 and 735 of 2009 claiming right of possession from Dienfa Limited through successive transfers cannot stand in the eye of law. In fact, the writ petitioners in collusion with each other fabricated all those documents and have been claiming interest in the disputed property. Therefore, the writ petitioners-respondents are bound to pay the arrear rents of the spaces used by them in the disputed plot No.7 as claimed by the government, as the government is the owner of the property in question on plot No.7 by operation of law. But the High Court Division most illegally made all the Rules absolute ousting the jurisdiction of the government to claim arrear rents.</u>
44. In view of the discussions made above and facts and circumstances of the cases, we are of the view that the High Court Division committed gross illegality in issuing Rules in Writ Petition Nos.1424, 723, 724, 725, 726, 727 and 735 of 2009 and making all the Rules absolute. Therefore, the judgments and orders dated 13-12-2009 and 14-12-2009 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos.1424, 723, 724, 725, 726, 727 and 735 of 2009 warrant interference by this Division.
45. In the light of the observations made above, we find merit in the submissions of the learned Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the appellants/petitioners in Civil Appeal and all the Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal.
46. Accordingly, the Civil Appeal No.179 of 2011 is allowed without any order as to costs. The judgment and order dated 13-12-2009 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.1424 of 2009 is hereby set-aside.
47. The Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal Nos. 280 of 2010, 1465-1470 of 2012 are disposed of in the light of the observations made in Civil Appeal No.179 of 2011.
The judgments and orders dated 13-12-2009 and 14-12-2009 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos.723, 724, 725, 726, 727 and 735 of 2009 are hereby set-aside.
End.

caseno:
Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.4549 of 2018.
(Arising out of CMP No.1161 of 2018)
lawyer:
Sk. Mohd. Murshed, Additional Attorney-General instructed by Sufta Khatun, Advocate-on-Record --------- For the Petitioners. 
Murad Reza, Senior Advocate instructed by Zainul Abedin, Advocate-on-Record --------- For the Respondents.
parties:
Government of Bangladesh and others ----- Petitioners
vs
Md Mainul Haque and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 1st day of August, 2018 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.8599 of 2018)
full_judgment:
M. Enayetur Rahim, J: Delay in filing the civil petition for leave to appeal is hereby condoned.
2. This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 01.08.2018 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.8599 of 2018 disposing the Rule with a direction to enlist the name of the writ petitioners-respondents in the monthly pay order (MPO) from the date of their joining within 01(one) month from the date of receipt of this order without any fail.
3. The facts, relevant for disposal of the instant leave petition are as follows:
The present respondents as petitioners filed writ petition No.8599 of 2018 under article 102 of the constitution of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh before the High Court Division seeking direction upon the present petitioners (hereinafter referred to as writ-respondents) to release the monthly pay order (MPO) with arrear and other service benefits from the date of their joining.
4. In the writ petition it is contended that the writ petitioners were appointed on different dates and joined in the vacant posts on different dates in different Schools as per the (বেসরকারী শিক্ষাপ্রতিষ্ঠানের (স্কুল ও কলেজ) জনবলকাঠামো ও এমপিও নীতিমালা, ২০১৩ to জনবলকাঠামো ও এমপিও নীতিমালা, ২০১৩) by following proper procedures, but the concerned authority has not yet released monthly pay order (MPO) of the writ petitioners despite their repeated request to the writ- respondents.
5. It is further contended that the writ-petitioners have spent long time in service with an unblemished service records and they fulfill all requirements for getting MPO as per (বেসরকারী শিক্ষাপ্রতিষ্ঠানের (স্কুল ও কলেজ) জনবলকাঠামো ও এমপিও নীতিমালা, ২০১৩ which has created “Legitimate expectation” in their favour to be enlisted under MPO. No proceeding was drawn against them. So, they are entitled to get the MPO and as such a direction should be given to the writ-respondents to take necessary steps for giving MPO to the petitioners.
6. The present petitioners, writ-respondents did not file any affidavit-in-opposition.
7. A Division Bench of the High Court Division after hearing the said Rule by the impugned judgment dated 01.08.2018 disposed of the same with a direction upon the writ-respondents to enlist the name of the writ petitioners in the monthly pay order from the date of their joining within a period of 1(one) month on receipt of the order without any fail.
8. Feeling aggrieved by the said judgment, the writ-respondents have filed this leave petition.
9. Mr. Sheikh Mohd. Morshed, learned Additional Attorney General, appearing for the petitioners having assailed the impugned judgment has made the following submissions:
I) the High Court Division without considering the provisions of relevant law/Nitimala directed the writ respondents to release the Government Portion of salary MPO of the writ petitioners from the date of their joining;
II) the writ petitioners were very much concerned about the law that there is no scope for the writ petitioners to get MPO, because as per ‘Janobol Khathamo’ the writ petitioners did not had/have any right to enjoy MPO benefit as their respective appointment was a temporary/conditional one;
III) the writ petitioners were appointed as an additional section teacher in different subjects in different institutions and in clause 6.11(b) of Janobol Khathamo- 2013 it is clearly stated as per the pattern of ‘Janobol Khathamo’ one subject teacher already got MPO benefit, therefore, for the same subject there is no scope to include another teacher in the MPO scheme, thus their prayer for MPO was rightly rejected;
IV) the MPO benefit depends upon the financial capacity of the government; it is a policy decision of the Government. After proper scrutiny when it was proved that the writ petitioners were out of patterns teacher, thus they are not entitled to get MPO;
V) as per pattern of the MPO scheme there is no vacant post in the said schools; the teachers and staffs who had requisite qualifications and patterned teachers, they have already been included in the MPO scheme, hence it is not possible to include the writ petitioners in MPO benefit.
10. On the other hand Mr. Murad Reza, learned Senior Advocate, appearing for the writ-petitioners-respondents having supported the impugned judgment has submitted that-
i) the High Court Division on proper consideration of the relevant law/Nitimala as well as the facts and circumstances of the present case rightly and lawfully has made the Rule absolute;
ii) the petitioners in response to the advertisement of NTRCA of the different posts participated in written and viva voce examination and successfully passed in the examination; annexure-A to writ petition shows that they are eligible to be appointed as Assistant Teacher of the respective subject at any Junior Secondary, Higher Secondary School, Madrasa in Bangladesh and according to section 10 of the Non-Government Teacher Registration and Certification Authority Act,2005 that বেসরকারী শিক্ষা প্রতিষ্ঠানের শিক্ষক নিয়োগের তালিকা প্রণয়ন, ২০০৫ one must be registered and certified by the authority and then they can be appointed as such the High Court Division legally directed the writ-respondents to enlist the name of the petitioners in the MPO for ends of justice.
11. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for the respective parties, perused the impugned judgment and other materials as placed before us.
12. The High Court Division in making the Rule has observed that-
“we have found that no proceeding has been pending against the petitioners nor any adverse report could be found against them and their colleagues/all teachers and staffs of their institution are enjoying monthly payment order (MPO) for same service they are same status like the petitioners. But even then the respondents remained silent without considering the petitioners claim and even did not give any reply. We have also found that the petitioners have been performing their duties till today. In that view of the matter we find substance in the Rule for consideration.”
13. Upon perusal of the impugned judgment it transpires that the High Court Division made the Rule absolute directing upon the writ-respondents to enlist the name of the petitioners in the MPO mainly on the view that their colleagues have already been enjoying MPO for same service and they were duly appointed in the service by the competent authority.
<u>14. As per the relevant Nitimala there is no scope to give MPO to a teacher who has been appointed out of pattern and the writ petitioners having been appointed as a non-MPO post against the section teacher and their claimed of MPO benefit by avoiding the said ‘Nitimala’ cannot be enforced.</u>
15. Further, in the case of Government represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Education and others Vs. Md. Saidur Rahman in Civil Petition for leave Appeal No.2584 of 2018 and Government of Bangladesh and others Vs. Md. Nazrul Islam and others, reported in 27 BLT page-167(AD) this Division has settled the issue involved in the present case and observed to the effect;
“In the case in hand, the petitioners did not allege that the writ-respondents have violated any legal right of them. The granting of MPO is the policy decision of the Government. Therefore, the petitioners could not claim the same as of right. This Division is of the view that teachers and staffs of the Non-Government School and College could not claim the MPO as a matter of right and as such, direction could not be given unless infringement of legal right or violation of law.”
16. Similar view has been expressed by this Division in the case of Government represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Education and others Vs. Md. Saidur Rahman in Civil Petition for Leave Appeal No.2584 of 2018;
17. In the above case it has been held that:
“Here, in this case, the High Court Division in fact, passed the impugned order to compel the executive to pay Government portion of salaries in as much as the Government did decide as yet to pay salaries to them or even did not assure them that the Government would pay the same. In absence of the statutory obligation, the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution is not justified in issuing mandamus for payment of salary since a mandamus cannot lie in the absence of a legal right based on the existence of statutory duty. The mere fact that recognition and institution have been granted to an institution or, for that matter, for conducting new course or subject a financial sanction. A financial liability cannot be foisted on the Government to reimburse the salary payable to the teachers and staffs of such presumption. No mandamus can issue for payment of salary by the Government in the absence of the prior sanction of the Government.”
“Accordingly to “Dicey”, Judges are not allowed to decide a case on the basis of whatever they consider just and fair. They are constrained by definite principles of law and by binding precedent.”
18. The High Court Division in passing the impugned judgment did not at all consider the above settled proposition of law and thus committed serious error of law in making the Rule.
19. In view of the above, we find merit in leave petition. Accordingly, the leave petition is disposed of.
The judgment and order dated 01.08.2018 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.8599 of 2018 is hereby set aside.
End.

lawyer:
Md Syed Mohidul Kabir, Advocate—For the Petitioners. 
Md Rafikul Hossain, with Md Nurul Islam chowdhury, Advocates—For the Opposite Party No.1.
parties:
Mohammad Ali being dead his heirs: 1(Ka) Majeda Khatun and others ------- Petitioners
VS
Tarapada Biswas and others -------- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
The instant Rule has been issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 3-10 and 16 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 19-6-2005 passed by the learned District Judge, Meherpur in Title Appeal No. 52 of 1995 affirming those dated 29-6-1995 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Meherpur in Title Suit No. 90 of 1985 dismissing the suit should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.
2. The petitioners herein as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 90 of 1985 before the then Subordinate Judge, Meherpur impleading the respondents-opposite parties as defendants for specific performance of contract for getting a registered deed of exchange for Ka schedule land but subsequently when exchange deed was registered on 27-64980 the plaintiffs inserted prayer for declaration of title as alternative prayer. Subsequently, plaintiffs inserted the prayer for recovery of Khas possession of the suit land except plot No.1601 and 1605.
3. The case of the plaintiffs, in brief is that suit land appertaining to CS Khatian Nos. 465, 1926, 1682, 468, 1747, 2042, 463 and 1614 originally belonged to Ram Das, Baman Das and Kishori Mohon in equal shares. Ram Das died leaving behind one son namely Tarapad Biswas and grandson Bijoy as his heirs. Baman Das died leaving behind son Narayan Chandra Biswas as his heir. Kishori Mohan died leaving behind two sons namely Kalipada and Monindra as his heirs. The plaintiffs who were Indian residents came to this country after partition in 1947 and made exchange with their Indian property with defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in respect of their 'Ka' schedule property on 10-6-1952. The said exchange was made by the plaintiffs' parents. The plaintiffs' predecessor got possession of `Ka' schedule property at the time of exchange. The exchange was made through General Power of Attorney. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 executed a Power of Attorney in favour of the plaintiffs' predecessors and it was revalidated in Miscellaneous Case No. 1846/52- 53. After the death of Mobarak Ali and his wife, the plaintiffs are in possession of 'Ka' schedule property as heirs. By way of exchange, the plaintiffs got 15.91 acres of land from the defendant Nos. 1 and 2. During the war of Liberation the said Power of Attorney executed by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 was lost and ultimately the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 executed another Power of Attorney in favour of the plaintiffs admitting earlier Power of Attorney at 10-6-1952 and it was revalidated in Miscellaneous Case No. 23/75-76. Having failed to get a regular deed of exchange from the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 the plaintiffs filed Miscellaneous Case No. 09/77-78 to the Kushtia Collectorate and upon hearing, the Deputy Commissioner rejected their prayer but allowed the prayer of the defendant Nos. 3-9, who also filed Miscellaneous Case No. 786(10/70-71 claiming 2/3 shares from the heirs of Ram Das and Baman Das by way of exchange. In fact, the defendant Nos. 3-9 made exchange with Ram Das's son Narayan in respect of 1/3rd share and they got possession of the same but their claim as regards 2/3rd interest of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 is false. The said defendants got the suit land collusively recorded in their names. Then on 20-8-1979 the Deputy Commissioner refused to entertain the plaintiffs' case and to grant them registered deed of exchange and hence the plaintiffs were compelled to file the suit on 6-9-1979. During pendency of the suit the defendant Nos. 3-8 and 9(Ka-Ca) dispossessed the plaintiffs on 4-5-1982 from the suit land except plot No. 1601 and 1605 wherein the plaintiffs got their abode.
4. The predecessor of defendant Nos. 3-8 namely Mojibur Rahman and the predecessor of defendant Nos. 9 (Ka-Ca) filed joint written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint contending inter alia that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and the suit is barred by limitation. Their specific case is that the suit land originally belonged to Ram Das, Baman Das and Kishori Mohan. The predecessor of Defendant Nos. 3-8 and the predecessor of defendant Nos. 9(Ka-Ca) exchanged their property situated in India with the property belonging to defendant Nos. 1 and 2 situated in Bangladesh on 11-5-1953. Similarly, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 exchanged their property situated in Bangladesh with the property belonged to the predecessor of defendant Nos. 3-8 situated in India on 27-1-1955. Accordingly, SA Record was prepared in the name of these defendants. They filed Miscellaneous Case in the Kushtia Collectorate with a view to register the said exchange deed and after due inquiry, the Deputy Commissioner, Kushtia granted genuineness certificate in favour of these defendants and registered the said deed of exchange on 27-6-1980. The further case of these defendants is that the plaintiffs who are distant relations of these defendants were given shelter in the house of these defendants and ultimately they created a Power of Attorney to grab the suit land belonged to the defendants. The defendants did not dispossess the plaintiffs from the suit land and, as such, the suit be dismissed.
5. The defendant No. 10, Government of Bangladesh filed a written statement denying the material allegation made in the plaint contending that the suit land originally belonged to Ram Das Biswas, Baman Das Biswas and Kishori Mohan in equal shares. Ram Das died leaving behind his son namely Tarapad and grandson Bijoy and Baman Das died leaving behind Narayan Chandra as his heirs. They went to India from the village of Dariapur under Meherpur District and the defendant No. 9, predecessor of defendant Nos. 9(Ka-Ca) came to Bangladesh who resided in village-Jitpur, Police Station-Tehotti, District-Nadia. In 1953 and 1954 they executed a Power of Attorney in favour of the predecessor of defendant Nos. 3-8 and 9(Ka-Ca). These defendants filed Miscellaneous Case No. 786(1c)/70-71 before the Deputy Commissioner with a view to register the deed of exchange which is allowed and the plaintiffs also filed miscellaneous case which was refused by Deputy Commissioner. The heirs of defendant Nos. 3-9 were in possession of the suit land on payment of rent to the Government and the plaintiffs have no right, title and interest over the suit land.
6. Mr Syed Mohidul Kabir, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that the trial court erroneously held that the plaintiffs did not disclose the date of cause of action of the suit but it is evident from the plaint that cause of action arose when the Assistant Custodian, Vested and Non-resident property, Kushtia refused Miscellaneous Case No.9 of 1977-1978 and the plaintiffs filed the suit within one month which is well within Article 113 of the Limitation Act and as cause of action is not a particular date rather bundle of facts which is required to be proved and, as such, findings of the trial court having affirmed by the appellate court on this score is not sustainable. He next submits that during pendency of title suit defendant No. 11, Assistant Custodian, Vested and Non-resident property, Kushtia executed the deed in favour of defendant Azizur Rahman and Mozibur Rahman on 25-6-1979, Exhibit E but such transfer does not debar the court to pass a decree to the plaintiffs for specific performance of contract and in a suit for specific performance of contract subsequent transfer to 3rd party does not effect the right of the parties and, as such, both the courts below committed error in not granting decree to the plaintiffs. Learned Advocate further submits that the trial court as well as the appellate court did not consider Exhibit 6, reports submitted by Revenue Deputy Collector, Kushtia after physical inquiry that the plaintiffs are in possession of homestead portion of the suit land and they got 1/3 share being owned by Ram Das but both the courts below overlooked that report and erroneously dismissed the suit which caused failure of justice. He further submits that Exhibit-7, certified copy of Miscellaneous Case No. 1846/52-53 clearly evidenced that the plaintiffs made exchange earlier in point of time whereby Mobari Mondal's exchange is clearly established but both the courts below failed to advert that aspect of the case and erroneously dismissed the suit which caused failure of justice. Learned Advocate further submits that Exhibit-4, irrevocable power of attorney executed by Tarapod Biswas and grandson Bijoy Kumar Biswas in favour of Mohammad Ali Mondal, son of late Mobari Mondal dated 3-5-1974 mentioning 'A schedule' of Bangladesh property and 'B schedule' of Indian property, but both the courts below did not consider that vital documents which caused failure of justice. Learned Advocate further submits that Mobari Mondal by Exhibit 5, certified copy of registered sale deed transferred his Indian property vide deed No. 13901/1960 in favour of Copal Chandra Mondal, Puma Chandra Mondal which also proves that Mobari Mondal got the suit land in exchange of his Indian property but both the courts below failed to put reliance upon that vital document and erroneously came to a wrong conclusion which caused failure of justice. He further submits that Exhibit-10, judgment of sessions case clearly proved that the petitioners' right of private defense has been clearly found and acquitted them from the charge of the case wherein the plaintiffs' mode of getting suit land has also been discussed which is clearly overlooked by both the courts below. Learned Advocate argued that the judgment of the courts below is outcome of misreading, non-reading and non-consideration of the material evidence produced by the petitioners and, as such, this Court should interfere for undoing the injustice perpetrated to the petitioners. Learned Advocate lastly submits that the trial court also did not discuss the oral evidence adduced by the plaintiffs wherefrom it is clearly apparent that the plaintiffs have got the suit land by virtue of exchange and the plaintiffs are entitled to get decree of specific performance. Learned Advocate in support of his contention referred the case of Syed Abul Haque and others vs Surendra Nath Majumder and others 59 DLR (AD) 111, Abdur Rajjak vs Monsur alom and others 1995 BLD (AD) 83, Sahabuddin Bhuiya vs Mather Mia and others 5 MLR (AD) 257, Hossain Ahmed Chowdhurij vs Nurul Amin 1996 BLD (AD) 31 = 47 DLR (AD) 162, Nur Mohammad vs Bangladesh 61 DLR (AD) 77, Sundar Ali vs Md Sirajul Hag 56 DLR 210, Surad Sarder vs Afjal Hossin 2 BLC (AD) 1947, Hafijur Rahman vs Banglasesh 1 BLC 25.7. Saifuddin Ahmed vs Dr. Hosneara Begum @ Golap and others 15 BLC 828, Anath Bondhu Goha and Sons Ltd. vs Babu Sudanshu Sekhor Haider 42 DLR (AD) 244, Rahima Akter vs Oshim Kumar Bosh and another 40 DLR (AD) 23, Yakub Ali and another vs Md Ali Akbor Hawlader and others 6 MLR (AD) 232, S Sibtaing Faijle vs Md Starfil Distubutors 16 DLR (SO 198, Abdul Majid Bepari vs Kahem Ali Molla 27 DLR 1, Dr. Gobinda and another vs Sreemoti Shanti Bai 3 SCC (1997) 419, forina Khatun and others vs Howladers and others 52 DLR 53, and Abdul Monab vs Joynul Abedin 10 BLC 361.
7. Mr Md Rafikul Hossain along with Md Nurul Islam Chowdhury, learned Advocates appearing for the opposite parties submits that Tarapad Biswas and Bijoy by deed dated 27-1-1955 exchanged the suit land with the predecessor of defendant Nos. 3-8 and 9 (Ka-Ca), Mojibur Rahman and Ajijur Rahman and similarly Mojibur Rahman and Ajijur Rahman on 11-5-1953 exchanged their Indian land with those persons and accordingly they filed Miscellaneous Case No. 786 (C-1) 1970-71 and accordingly Collector of Kushtia executed and registered deed in favour of them on 27-6-1980 and rejected the plaintiffs' miscellaneous case and, as such, the present suit of the plaintiffs is not maintainable. Learned Advocate further submits that record of right has been prepared in the name of the defendants finding their title and possession in the suit land during S.A operation and, as such, plaintiffs' suit is not maintainable in the present form. He further submits that although the plaintiffs' claim that Ammoktarnama deed was executed on 1-6-1952 with defendant Nos. 1 & 2 and a further claim that during Liberation War their documents were lost, but they could not produce even certified copies of those documents and pointing those infirmity, the Collector of Kushtia rejected their claim for validation of their deed and, as such, the plaintiffs are not entitled to get any relief in the instant matter. He further submits that the claim of dispossession of the plaintiffs from the suit land is also not on substantiated on evidence, rather the defendants got possession of the suit land in 1953 and since then they have been holding and possessing the same and both the courts below also affirmed those facts. Learned Advocate further submits that the plaintiffs being distant relations of defendants are in possession in plot No. 1601 and 1605 as licensee whereby they cannot claim title therein. He also submits that the plaintiffs' suit is clearly barred by limitation having found by both the courts below and, as such, the instant suit is not maintainable. Learned advocate argued that the defendants have been paying rent of the suit land and submitted numerous Dakhilas which prove that they are in possession of the suit land which also negate the claim of the plaintiffs. Learned advocate argued that witnesses of the plaintiffs failed to prove plaintiffs' title and possession over the suit land and subsequent dispossession therefrom which have been highlighted by both the courts below and, as such, plaintiffs are not entitled to get any relief in the instant suit. Learned advocate avers that the defendants have been holding and possessing 2/3 shares of the suit khatian having shares of Bamon Das, Ram Das while 'Kishori Mohon's 1/3 share is being possessed by Mithun Mandol and, as such, plaintiffs' claim of title and possession is clearly disproved which have been highlighted by both the courts below. Learned advocate pointed that the plaintiffs failed to prove any misreading, non-reading and non-consideration of the evidence by the courts below and, as such, in absence of such error the present revisional application is not maintainable. Learned advocate submits that concurrent findings of fact in absence of any infirmity are immune from interference from the revisional court and, as such, Rule is liable to be discharged. Learned advocate lastly submits that the exhibits filed by the defendants are clear evidence of the title and possession of the defendants of the suit land and, as such, Rule is liable to be discharged. Learned advocate in support of his contention referred the case of Bangladesh represented by DC Pabna and others vs Abdus Sobhan Talukder and another reported in 42 DLR (AD) 63, Abdul Khalek vs Government of Bangladesh (2016) 1 LNJ 305 = 22 BLC 738, Amanut Ullah and others vs Ali Mohammad Bhuiya and another reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 199 = 2 BLC (AD) 134, 21 DLR 918, 5 MLR (AD) 329 = 5 BLC (AD) 189, 9 BLD 352, 47 DLR 441 and 56 DLR 39.
8. Having gone through the pleadings, impugned judgments, annexures and other materials it appears that the suit land along with other land belonged to Ram Das, Bamon Das and Kishori Mohan, each holding 1/3 share. Ram Das died leaving behind one son Tarapodo and grandson Bijoy Kumar who got Ram Das's share. Bamon Das survived by Narayon Chandra who got 1/3 share and Kishori Mohan died leaving two sons Kali Podo and Monindra who also got 1/3 share. According to plaintiff, Tara Podo and Bijoy Kumar exchanged the Ka schedule land with Mobarak Ali alias Mobari Ali and Gole Jan who exchanged Kha schedule land with Tara Podo and Bijoy Kumar. Due to complex situation Mobari Ali and Gule Jan on 10-6-1952 executed a power of attorney in favour of Tara Podo and Bijoy Kumar while Tara Podo and Bijoy Kumar also executed a power of attorney in favour of Mobari Ali who validated said power of attorney from Kushtia collectorate vide Miscellaneous Case No. 1846 of 52-53 and while owning and possessing they died leaving behind the plaintiffs but during liberation war they lost the said power of attorney for which Tara Podo and Bijoy Kumar again executed a Notarized power of attorney on 30-5-1974 mentioning the earlier power of attorney dated 10-6-1952 which the plaintiff validated from Kushtia collectorate vide Misc. Case No. 23/75-76 and in the suit called for the registered records whereupon Md Abu Taller, Assistant Record Keeper of Kustia Deputy Commissioner office came with the records and deposed as PW.5. Register of Validation Case No.1846 / 1952-53 was marked as Exhibit 7 and proceeding of Miscellaneous case being case No. 7860-1) 70-71 and 09/77-78 were marked as Exhibit 11 and 12 respectively.
9. On perusal of Exhibit 11 and 12 it appears that RDC, Kushtia inquired into the matter and submitted report on 20-12-1978 to the effect that plaintiffs are in possession of 1/3 land and the defendants are also in possession of 1/3 land but there is no reflection of such findings in order dated 28-8-1979 while rejecting plaintiffs' exchange deed No. 9/77-78 and the trial court as well as the appellate Court did not advert that aspect of the case.
10. Now it is to be looked into whether the plaintiffs were dispossessed from the suit land except plot No.1601 and 1605. The defendants admitted plaintiffs' possession in plot No. 1601 and 1605 with contention that the plaintiffs being their distant relations they were allowed to reside therein as licensee but in the report submitted by RDC in Misc. Case No. 786/70-71 and 09/77-78 RDC it is mentioned that the plaintiffs are in possession of the share of Tara Podo and Bijoy.
11. The trial Court held that there is no cause of action of the suit mentioning an incident referred to in the plaint. But cause of action is bundles of facts to be proved during trial by adducing evidence. Isolated single incident is not determinant factor for cause of action rather it consists of entire set of facts which gives rise a legal action, to be proved by the plaintiff. But the trial court as well as the appellate court failed to advert and consider that vital aspect of the case. In 2 BLC AD 47 our Apex Court held that:
"The term "cause of action" has not been defined in the Code of Civil Procedure. Rule 1(e) of Order VII of the Code only provides that besides other particulars, mentioned in different clauses of Rule 1, the plaint shall contain the "facts constituting the cause of action and when it arose". The cause of action for the suit ordinarily thus, means the cause which leads the plaintiffs to bring a legal action.
The incidence of cause of action must be antecedent to the bringing of the suit at a time when the right to sue arose for the first time. It consists of the entire set of facts which gives rise to a legal action and is to be proved to entitle the plaintiff to succeed in the suit. It has little relation either to the defence to be taken by the defendant or the nature of relief to be prayed for by the plaintiff in the suit."
12. On perusal of Exhibit 7, certified copy of Miscellaneous Case No. 1846/1952-53 it appears that prayer was made by the plaintiffs' predecessor Mobari Mondal for getting the documents re-stamped and the documents were made over to the party after disposing the case. So from that documents it appears that Mobari Mondal filed case for re-stamping documents much earlier as disclosed in the plaint but both the Court below failed to rely upon that vital document without any logical ground. Similarly Miscellaneous Case No. 788/1953-54 filed by the predecessor of the defendants has been disposed of. But on perusal of the Exhibit 8, information slip submitted by the plaintiffs, it appears that no such miscellaneous case being No. 788/1953-54 was available in the office.
13. On perusal of the certified copy of the judgment of the Sessions Case No. 156 of 1980, Exhibit-10 it appears that the defendants were informant therein wherein present petitioners were accused and learned Additional Sessions Judge in his judgment dated 29-11-1982 held that as per statement of PW 1 it is revealed that both parties suffered casualties in the occurrence and accused persons were exercising their right of private defence. The accused person cannot therefore be found guilty of the charge leveled against them in this case. Learned Additional Sessions Judge also found that northern portion of the disputed plot belongs to Mobari Mondal. Learned judge also concluded that prosecution side in fact got no possession in the disputed plot. However the Court opined that disputes of title and possession is to be settled in civil suit pending before the Court of law.
14. On perusal of Exhibit 5, it appears that Mobari Mondal and Gule Jan Bibi transferred their Indian land by deed No. 13901 of 1960 which is a strong evidence that they have exchanged property and got property of erstwhile East-Pakistan. These facts and circumstances and evidentiary value of documentary evidences were not evaluated and discussed by the courts below.
15. Both the parties paid rents in the name of recorded owners which were marked as exhibits. PW 1, Md Yeasin Hossain in his evidence narrated all the facts and circumstances graphically and stated also the date of dispossession. He also stated that he was dispossessed on 5th March 1982 and he also denied that they are licensee under the defendants. PW 2, Md Abul Hossain stated that he found plaintiffs' possession while the defendants dispossessed the plaintiffs. PW 3, Fazhil Hague also proved possession and dispossession of the plaintiffs. PW 4, Md Ayub Hossain, son of Mithun Mondal who is admitted owner of 1/3 share of Kishori Mohan stated that there was an exchange between the plaintiffs'-predecessor and Tara Pada and Bijay Kumar in the month of Chaitra, 1356 BS and plaintiffs were dispossessed in 5th March, 1982 from the suit land except Plot Nos. 1600, 1601 and 1605. He denied the suggestion that there was no exchange between the parties. He stated that Mojibur Rahman did not exchange any property with Tara Pado and Bijoy, he denied the suggestion that plaintiffs are licensee in Plot No. 1600, 1601 and 1605. The said PW4 is a vital witness for both the parties as because the defendants also stated that Mithun Mondal got 1/3 property of recorded owners. PW 5, Md Abu Taher, an employee of DC office who brought register of the case No. 1846/1952-53, which proves that there was an Register in respect of aforesaid case which has been produced before the Court. DW 1, Mohibur Rahman, son of Mojibur Rahman stated in his deposition that his uncle exchanged the homestead of Dr. Rashid wherein they have been residing, there was homestead of Ram Das, Bamon Das and Kishori Mohan in Plot Nos. 1601 and 1605 wherein they have 2/3rd share and the plaintiffs are licensee therein. So it is clearly apparent that the defendants are residing in the homestead of Dr. Rashid while the plaintiffs are living in Plot Nos. 1601 and 1605. He admitted that Mithun Mondal got 1/3rd share of Kishori Mohan. He also admitted that previously Monazat Ali and Mobari Mondal resided in Plot No. 1605 and he admitted that he does not know about exchange deed dated 10-6-1952 of Mobari Mondal and also does not know whether the deed was validated from Kushtia Collectoriate in Miscellaneous Case No. 846/1952-53 and also does not know whether power of attorney of Mobari Mondal was lost in 1971. He admitted that his father and uncle started residing Dr. Rashid's homestead on getting it by exchange where they still residing. He stated that his father and uncle lived jointly. DW 2, Md Nafor Uddin stated that Ajizur Rahman and Mojibur Rahman resided in the homestead of Dr. Rashid by exchange. He cannot say how many plots are in the suit land. DW-3, Md Nafal Uddin, son of late Asel Uddin stated that he heard about exchange between Tara Pado and Bijoy with Azijur Rahman and Mojibur Rahman. He stated that Azijur Rahman and Mojibur Rahman lived in the homestead of Dr. Rashid since 1950. The father in law of defendant No. 4, Arshad Ali stated that he does not know with whom Ajizur Rahman and Mojibur Rahman exchanged property. He does not know except Dr. Rashid and Narayan. He although disclosed that he has 18 Bigha land but could not disclose plot Numbers. DW-5, Md Ismail stated that plaintiffs never possessed the suit land but he cannot say the boundary of the suit land. He cannot say his properties except one plot although claimed that he has 12 Bighas of land.
16. From the above discussions, oral and documentary evidences it is amply clear that the trial court as well as the appellate court failed to discuss the documentary as well as oral evidence of the parties in material particulars and arrived at a wrong conclusion upon misreading, non-reading and non-consideration of evidence of the parties. It is fairly established that when there is misconstruction of document and also misreading and non-consideration of documents, even though the judgments of the courts below are concurrent, the revisional court can interfere with such findings. In 59 DLR AD 111 it is held that:
"In repelling the contention of the learned counsel of the appellants that High Court Division exceeded its jurisdiction while making the Rule absolute upon interfering with the finding of fact arrived at by the last Court of fact, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-respondent has submitted that when the finding of fact arrived at is result of misreading and non-consideration of the evidence or misconstruction of the document the High court Division is quite competent to set-aside the finding of fact so arrived at by the last Court of fact. In support of the aforesaid contention, the learned counsel for the plaintiff-respondents has referred to the case reported in 48 DLR (AD) 154 and 57 DLR (AD) 55. The principle of law enunciated in the case referred to by the learned Counsel of the plaintiff-respondents is applicable to the facts and circumstances of the instant case."
17. In 5 MLR AD 256 it is also held that:
"A perusal of the judgment of the High Court Division shows that the learned judge had discussed the evidence on record threadbare and pointed out that the appellate Court left out of consideration important pieces of evidence and palpably misconstrued the evidence that it had considered. The learned judge also pointed out that the conclusion reached by the appellate Court on title and possession is absurd. He was, however, quite mindful of the fact that usually in revisional jurisdiction the Court is not expected to go into evidence but that the instant case is an exception to the Rule. The appellate Court having absolutely misconstrued the evidence we do not find any tangible fault with the elaborate judgment of the High Court division. "
<u>18. It appears that the plaintiffs are in possession in Plot No. 1601 and 1605 which is admitted by the defendants although the defendants claimed that the plaintiffs are licensee under the defendants, but the defendants failed to substantiate their such claim. It is further proved that the defendants never possessed plot Nos. 1601 and 1605 at any point of time rather they lived in the homestead of Dr. Rashid. So it is amply clear that from the very inception, the plaintiffs are in possession in plot Nos. 1601 and 1605. The exchange executed between the plaintiffs and the heirs of Ram Das is clearly established. From the documentary evidence such facts are also established.
