(Arising out of Writ Petition Nos. 4006-4008 of 2019) And
(Arising out of Writ Petition Nos. 5096-5097 of 2019)
(From the judgment and orders dated 06.11.2019 and 27.11.2019 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 4006-4008 of 2019 and Writ Petition Nos. 5096-5097 of 2019 respectively).
full_judgment:
Borhonuddin J. Delay of 81 days in filing the civil petition for leave to appeal nos.278-280 of 2020 is condoned. 

2. Since question of law involve is identical and facts are almost similar as such all the civil petitions have been taken together for hearing and disposed of by this common judgment. 

3. Facts relevant for disposal of all the civil petitions in brief are that the respondents in Writ Petition Nos.4006-4008 of 2019 herein as petitioners and the petitioner in Writ Petition Nos.5096-5097 of 2019 herein as petitioner filed separate applications under article 102(2) of the constitution challenging failure of the writ respondents to make final assessment of the petitioner's imported consignment within the stipulated time of 120 working days from the date of provisional assessment as prescribed under section 81(2) of the Customs Act and further seeking direction upon the writ-respondents to return the Bank Guarantee furnished by the importer-petitioners at the time of provisional assessment for failure of the respondents to make final assessment within the timeframe. 

4. In Writ Petition No.4006 of 2019 it is contended that the petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 11.12.2017 for importation of 'Seamless Pipe ASTM' declaring H.S. Code No.7304.31.00; After arrival of the goods at Chattogram Port, the petitioner through his C&F Agent submitted Bill of Entry No.C-427603 dated 18.03.2018 for releasing the goods as per declaration but the customs authority disputed the declared H.S. Code and suggested that the applicable H.S. Code for the imported goods would be 7304.90.00 instead of declared 7304.31.00; But on the request of the petitioner, customs authority released the goods upon provisional assessment under section 81 of the Customs Act on 27.05.2018; Thereafter 209 days have been elapsed but the customs authority failed to make final assessment within the stipulated time. Hence the petitioner constrained to file the writ petition seeking direction to return the Bank Guarantee furnished at the time of provisional assessment. 

5. Upon hearing the petitioner a Division Bench of the High Court Division issued a Rule Nisi upon the respondents with a direction to maintain status-quo in respect of encashment of the Bank Guarantee. 

6. Learned Assistant Attorney General without filing any affidavit-in-opposition contested the Rule on behalf of the respondent no.1 stating interalia that the imported goods have been released by the customs authority on provisional assessment at the instance of the importer-petitioner but the petitioner did not deposit expenses for chemical examination of the goods as required under section 200 of the Act on time and for that reason the respondent-customs authority could not complete chemical examination of the goods in time as such the petitioner cannot claim any benefit for his-own fault. 

7. After contested hearing, the High Court Division made the Rule absolute directing the Writ Respondent No.1 to return the Bank Guarantee infavour of the petitioner within 30 days. 

8. Feeling aggrieved, the writ respondents as petitioners preferred instant Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.278 of 2020. 

9. In Writ Petition No.4007 of 2019 the writ petitioner contended that he opened a Letter of Credit dated 05.04.2016 for importing 'Seamless Pipe ASTM' declaring H.S. Code No.7304.29.20; After arrival of the goods at Chattogram port, the petitioner through his C&F Agent submitted Bill of Entry No.C-1050615 dated 29.08.2016 for releasing the goods as per declaration but the customs authority did not release the goods disputing declared H.S. Code and suggested that the applicable H.S. Code would be 7304.90.00 instead of declared 7304.29.20, however released the goods on provisional assessment dated 06.09.2016 under section 81 of the Customs Act subject to final assessment as per chemical test report by the BUET; Though the BUET sent the test report on 21.06.2017 but the respondent did not complete the final assessment despite the application filed by the petitioner; Hence the petitioner constrained to file the writ petition. 

10. Upon nearing the petitioner a Division Bench of the High Court Division issued' a Rule Nisi upon the respondents with a direction to maintain status-quo in respect of encashment of the Bank Guarantee. 

11. Learned Assistant Attorney General without filing any affidavit-in-opposition contested the Rule on behalf of the respondent no.1 stating interalia that the imported goods have been released by the customs- authority on provisional assessment at the instance of the petitioner but the petitioner did not deposit expenses for chemical examination of the goods as required under section 200 of the Act on time and for that reason the respondents-customs authority could not complete chemical examination of the goods in time. As such the petitioner cannot claim any benefit for his own fault. 

12. After hearing the parties, the High Court Division made the Rule absolute with a direction to the Writ Respondent No.1 to return the Bank Guarantee infavour of the petitioner within 30 days. 

13. Feeling aggrieved, the writ-respondents as petitioners preferred instant Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.279 of 2020. 

14. In Writ Petition No.4008 of 2019 it is contended that the petitioner opened Letter of Credit dated 27.10.2016 for importing 'Seamless Pipe ASTM' declaring H.S. Code No.7304.23.20; After arrival of the goods at Chattogram port, the petitioner through his C&F Agent submitted Bill of Entry No.C-150121 dated 31.01.2017 for releasing the goods as per declaration but the customs authority raised dispute regarding the H.S. Code and suggested that the applicable H.S. Code of the imported goods would be 7304.90.00 instead of declared 7304.23.00; However at the instance of the petitioner the goods were released on provisional assessment under section 81 of the Customs Act vide order dated 19.02.2017; Though BUET sent the test report on 07.06.2017 but the customs authority did not refund the Bank Guarantee despite application filed by the petitioner. Hence the petitioner con-strained to file the writ petition. 

15. Upon hearing the petitioner a Division Bench of the High Court Division issued a Rule Nisi upon the respondents with a direction to maintain status-quo in respect of encashment of the Bank Guarantee. 

16. Learned Assistant Attorney General without filing any affidavit-in-opposition contested the Rule on behalf of the respondent no.1 and submitted interalia that the goods have been released by the customs authority on provisional assessment at the instance of the petitioner but the petitioner did not deposit expenses for chemical examination of the goods as required under section 200 of the Act on time and as such the customs authority could not complete chemical examination of the goods in time; Hence the petitioner cannot claim any benefit for his own fault. 

17. After hearing the parties, a Division Bench of the High Court Division made the Rule absolute directing the respondent no.1 to return the Bank Guarantee infavour of the petitioner within 30 days. 

18. Feeling aggrieved, the writ-respondents as petitioners preferred instant Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.280 of 2020. 

19. In Writ Petition No.5096 of 2019 it is contended that the petitioner opened a Letter of Credit on 30.07.2018 for importing 'Black Steel Seamless Pipe' declaring H.S. Code No.7304.29.10 and 7304.29.20; After arrival of the goods at ICD Kamlapur, Dhaka, the petitioner through his C&F Agent submitted Bill of Entry No.C-28719 dated 18.10.2018 for releasing the goods as per declaration but the customs authority raised dispute regarding the declared H.S. Code suggesting different H.S. Code and also suggested to examine the goods by the BUET for determining actual H.S Code; Though the provisional assessment was made on 21.10.2018 but the respondent no.1 sent a letter to the petitioner on 10.04.2019 asking to deposit required money for chemical examination beyond the period of limitation; Hence the petitioner constrained to file the writ petition. 

20. Upon hearing the petitioner, a Division Bench of the High Court Division issued a Rule Nisi upon the respondents with a direction to maintain status-quo in respect of encashment of the Bank Guarantee. 

21. The respondent no.1 contested the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition denying averments of the petitioner in the writ petition and stating interalia that the petitioner's C&F Agent on 18.10.2018 filed an application to the respondent no.1 requesting him to draw sample of the imported goods and send the same to BCSIR in order to determine the actual H.S. Code and also requested to release the goods on provisional assessment under section 81 of the Customs Act; Accordingly, the respondents allowed the petition and assessed the goods provisionally on 21.10.2018; The respondent-customs authority sent sample of the goods to the BCSIR Lab on 27.11.2018 for chemical examination and informed the BCSIR authority that cost of sample test would be paid by the importer-petitioner under section 200 of the Customs Act but the petitioner did not pay the cost to the BCSIR; Being informed about the same the respondent no.2 wrote a letter to the petitioner on 10.04.2019 to deposit the Cost within 10 days but the petitioner did not pay heed. As such the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

22. After hearing the parties and perusing the record a Division Bench of the High Court Division discharged the Rule and vacated the order of status-quo granted earlier by judgment and order dated 27.11.2019. 

23. Feeling aggrieved, the writ-petitioner preferred instant Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1368 of 2020. 

24. In Writ Petition No.5097 of 2019 it is contended that the petitioner opened a Letter of Credit on 30.07.2018 for importing 'Black Steel Seamless Pipe' declaring H.S. Code No.7304.29.10 and 7304.29.20; After arrival of the goods at ICD Kamlapur, Dhaka, the petitioner through his C&F Agent submitted Bill of Entry No.C-28697 dated 17.10.2018 for releasing the goods as per declaration but the customs authority raised dispute regarding declared H.S. Code and suggested different H.S. Codes and also suggested that the sample of the goods is required to be examined by the BUET for determining actual H.S. Code; However, at the instance of the petitioner the goods were released on provisional assessment under section 81 of the Customs Act vide order dated 21.10.2018; After expiry of the statutory period of limitation the respondent no.1 sent a letter on 10.04.2019 asking the petitioner to deposit required money for chemical examination of the sample by BUET in order to determine the actual H.S Code; Hence the petitioner constrained to file the writ petition. 

25. Upon hearing the petitioner, a Division Bench of the High Court Division issued a Rule Nisi upon the respondents with a direction to maintain status-quo in respect of encashment of the Bank Guarantee. 

26. The respondent no.1 contested the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition denying material allegations made in the writ petition and contending interalia that the petitioner's C&F Agent wrote an application dated 18.10.2018 to the respondent no.1 requesting him to draw sample of the imported goods and send it to the BCSIR for chemical examination to ascertain the actual H.S. Code and also. requested to release the goods assessing provisionally under section 81 of the Customs Act; The respondents allowed the application and released the goods upon provisional assessment on 21.10.2018; Sample of the goods have been sent to BCSIR Lab on 14.01.2019 by the customs authority and informed the BCSIR that the cost of the test would be paid by the petitioner under section 200 of the Customs Act; But the petitioner did not pay the cost; The respondent no.2 vide letter dated 10.04.2019 requested the petitioner to deposit the cost but to no avail. As such the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

27. After hearing the parties the High Court Division discharged the Rule and vacated the status-quo granted earlier vide judgment and order dated 27.11.2019. 

28. Feeling aggrieved, the writ-petitioner .preferred instant Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1369 of 2020. 

29. Mr. Sk. Md. Morshed learned Additional Attorney General by filing an additional paper book in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.278 of 2020. arising out of Writ Petition No. 4006 of 2019 submits that though the goods were released upon provisional assessment dated 27.05.2018 at the instance of the petitioner on condition that sample of the imported goods would be examined by the BUET for ascertaining actual H.S. Code at the cost of the petitioner under section 200 of the Customs Act but the petitioner paid the cost amount through pay order dated 08.06.2018 and the department of Materials and Metallurgical Engineering (MME), BUET, sent the test report on 27.08.2018, based on the report the respondent no.1 issued a show cause notice upon the petitioner on 25.02.2019 stating that the petitioner declared wrong H.S. Code for evading customs duties, VAT and other charges and asked the petitioner to pay the amount affording an opportunity to reply and hearing. 

30. Mr. Morshed continues that from the pay order dated 08.06.2018 and test report of BUET annexed to the supplementary affidavit it is apparent that due to negligence of the petitioner in paying the cost for chemical examination and time consumed for chemical examination by the BUET the prescribed timeframe cannot be maintained. Furthermore, it is apparent from the test report by the BUET that the writ petitioner declared wrong H.S. Code for evading applicable duties and taxes as per actual H.S. Code of the imported goods but this aspect was not considered by the High Court Division in passing the impugned judgment and order as such impugned judgment and order is not tenable in the eye of law. He also submits that it appears from annexure-'H' appended to the Writ Petition No.4007 of 2019 (Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.279 of 2020) that provisional assessment was done on 06.09.2016 at the instance of the petitioner and accordingly sample of the goods sent to the BUET for determining actual H.S. Code wherein it is found that the declared H.S. Code by the petitioner was wrong and even the description of the goods was also wrong and the petitioner declared the wrong H.S. Code with wrong description of the goods for evading applicable duties and taxes on the actual H.S. Code. He next submits that due to negligence of the petitioner in depositing the cost for chemical examinations as well as time spend in chemical examination by BUET the period of limitation could not be maintained and this factual aspect was not considered by the High Court Division as such impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. 

31. The learned Additional Attorney General further submits that the provisional assessment has been done in Writ Petition No.4008 of 2019 (Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.280 of 2020) on 19.02.2017 but due to negligence of the petitioner in depositing cost of the chemical examinal and time consumed in the process of chemical examination stipulated timeframe cannot be maintained. 

32. By referring annexure-'G' and 'H', he also submits that the petitioner earlier filed Writ Petition No.18820 of 2017, upon hearing the petitioner a Division Bench of the High Court Division issued a Rule Nisi upon the respondents with a direction to dispose of application dated 14.12.2017 filed by the petitioner for refunding the Bank Guarantee amount and accordingly the respondent no.1 disposed of the application stating interalia that the BUET determined H.S. Code of the imported goods as manifest that the petitioner declared wrong H.S Code for evading duties and taxes. Thereafter, the petitioner filed the present writ petition but the High Court Division lost sight of the above facts and erroneously passed the impugned judgment and order which is not sustainable in the eye of law. 

33. On the other hand Mr. Reja-E-Rabbi appearing on behalf of the respondent nos.1 and 2 in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos.278-280 in support of the impugned judgment and orders passed by the High Court Division submits that the statutory time limit for final assessment is 120 working days under section 81(2) of the Customs Act and as such the customs authority is duty bound to make the provisional assessment final within the statutory timeframe, failure of which liable to adjust or refund the amount or guarantee to the importer/exporter. In support of his submission learned advocate referred to the case of Government of Bangladesh and others vs. Md. Salim Hossain, reported in 11 BLT (AD) 2003. 

34. Heard the learned Additional Attorney General and the learned Advocate for the respondents in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos.278-280 of 2020. Perused the papers/documents contained in the paper books. 

35. In Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos.1368-1369 of 2020. Mr. Reza-E-Rabbi appearing for the petitioner submits that the High Court Division erred in law in not considering that section 81(2) of the Customs Act mandates to make final assessment within 120 working days from the date of provisional assessment but the respondents failed to make final assessment within the timeframe. He also submits that the High Court Division failed to consider that the respondents most illegally vide letter dated 10.04.2019 asked the petitioner to deposit cost for chemical examination long after the provisional assessment as such the impugned judgment and orders are liable to be set aside. He also submits that though section 200 of the Customs Act requires the petitioner to pay cost of the chemical examination but non-payment of the same is not a bar for the respondents to make the provisional assessment final under section 81 of the Customs Act. 

36. On the other hand, Mr. Sk. Md. Morshed learned Additional Attorney General supports the impugned judgment and orders passed by the High Court Division. 

37. Heard the learned Advocate for the petitioner and learned Additional Attorney General for the respondents. Perused the papers/documents contained in the paper books. 

38. We have gone through the impugned judgment and order passed in all the writ petitions. The moot question is to be decided whether the customs authority is liable to make the provisional assessment final under section 81(2) of the Customs Act within the time stipulated therein despite non-cooperation or negligence or wrong declaration by the importer-petitioner. Section 81 of the Customs Act reproduced below: 
"81. Provisional assessment of duty-(1) Where it is not possible immediately to assess the customs duty that may be payable on any imported goods entered for home consumption or for warehousing or for clearance from a warehouse for home consumption, or on any goods entered for exportation, for the reason that the goods required chemical or other test [or a further enquiry] for purposes of assessment, or that all the documents or Complete documents or full information pertaining to those goods have not been furnished, an officer not below the rank of [Assistant Commissioner of Customs] may order that the duty payable on such goods be assessed provisionally: 
Provided that the importer (same in the case of goods entered for ware-housing) or the exporter pays such additional amount as security or furnishes such guarantee of a schedule bank for the payment thereof as the said officer deems sufficient to meet the excess of the final assessment of duty over the provisional assessment. 
(2) Where any goods are allowed to be cleared or delivered on the basis of such provisional assessment, the amount of duty actually payable on those goods shall, [within a period of one hundred and twenty working days from the date of the provisional assessment], be finally assessed and on completion of such assessment the appropriate officer shall order that the amount already paid or guaranteed be adjusted against the amount payable on the basis of final assessment, and the difference between them shall be paid forthwith to or by the importer or exporter as the case may be: 
[Provided that the Board may under exceptional circumstances recorded in writing, extend the period of final assessment specified under this sub-section.]" 

39. Again, section 200 of the Customs Act runs as follows: 
"200. Owner to make all arrangements and bear all expenses-Any opening, unpacking, waiving[?], measuring, re-packing, bulking, sorting, letting, marking, numbering, loading, unloading, carrying or laiding[?] of goods or their' containers for the purposes of or incidental to, the [examination, including any investigation, scientific or chemical test or draft survey, by an officer of Customs, removal or warehousing thereof shall be done, and any facilities or assistance required for any such examination, investigation, test or survey shall be provided, by or at the expense of the owner of the goods]." 

40. In the cases in hand, it appears that provisional assessments were done at the instance of the importer-petitioners. The 'C&F Agent of the importer filed application for provisional assessment of the goods and also prayed for chemical examination of the same. Accordingly, the petitioner released the goods on payment of duties and taxes in cash as per his declaration and furnished Bank Guarantee for the differential amount of duties and taxes between the declared H.S Code and suggested H.S Code by the customs authority. Thereafter, the customs authority sent the sample for chemical examination to the Lab of BCSIR or BUET as suggested by the C&F Agent of the importer. According to section 200 of the Customs Act the owner/importer shall have to bear all expenses for examination including any investigation, scientific or chemical test, amongst others, for the imported goods. The language of section 200 mandates the provision of law with the word 'shall'. So from the language of section 200 it is evident that the expenses for chemical examination shall be borne by the importer/owner of the goods. 

41. Similarly, section 81(2) stipulated the timeframe for making provisional assessment final with the word 'shall'. Section 81 provides that the National Board of Revenue may, under exceptional circumstances recorded in writing, extend the period of final assessment specified under this sub-sections. From Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos.278-280 of 2020 arising out of Writs Petition Nos.4006- 4008 of 2019, it is evident that though the provisional assessments were made at the instance of the petitioner's C&F Agent who applied in writing for releasing the goods on provisional assessment subject to ascertaining actual H.S. Code through chemical examination by the BUET/ BCSIR but from the annexures appended to the writ petitions it is apparent that the C&F agent of the petitioner did not deposit the expense of chemical examination in time. Moreover, chemical examination by the BUET/BCSIR consumed some time for which the timeframe cannot be maintained. Moreover, in the chemical examination it is proved that the petitioner imported the goods by declaring wrong H.S. Code in order to evade duties and taxes. Thereafter, the customs authority issued show cause notice upon the importer-petitioner referring chemical examination report by giving opportunity to reply and hearing but the petitioner without giving reply or appearing in hearing i.e. without exhausting the adjudication process invoked the writ jurisdiction. The High Court Division lost sight of this factual and legal aspect and thus came to erroneous decision in making the Rules absolute. Though there is statutory time limit under section 81(2) of the Customs Act to make provisional assessment final but from the chemical examination report it appears that the importer-petitioner intentionally tried to deceive the Government from realizing revenue by declaring wrong H.S. Code of the imported goods which tantamounts to practicing fraud. It is the settled principle of law that action against fraud has no limitation. Accordingly, the impugned judgment and orders passed in, Writ Petition Nos.4006- 4008 of 2019 passed by the High Court Division are hereby set aside. 

42. In other two Writ Petitions i.e. 5096-5097 of 2019 the High Court Division after thorough discussions rightly arrived at a decision that: 
"Due to willful negligence on part of the petitioner to pay chemical examination expenses fee to the BCSIR as required under section 200 of the Act, the respondent Customs authority did not collect the test report for the purpose of final assessment of the goods in question. Such acts of the petitioner are not tenable in the eye of law. Consequently, the petitioner is barred from seeking any relief under Article 102 of the Constitution on the plea that the final assessment has/had not been done by the customs authority within 120 (one hundred and twenty) working days as prescribed under section 81(2) of the Act, 1969.' 

43. Thus judgment and orders passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 5096-5097 of 2019 are maintained. 

44. Accordingly, all the civil petitions for leave to appeal are disposed of. 

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 27.06.2001 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.3630 of 1999)
full_judgment:
Md. Nuruzzaman J.: This Civil Appeal, by leave, has arisen out of the judgment and order dated 27.06.2001 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.3630 of 1999 disposing of the Rule Nisi with observation that the writ-petitioners are poor people and entitled to get alternative plots on proving their prima facie title and ownership in the land in question and with a direction to the requiring body to finalize the Land Acquisition (in short L.A.) cases within 6(six) months from the date of receipt of the order, till the finalization, the parties are directed to maintain status quo in respect of the possession of the lands.
 
2. Facts leading to filing of this civil appeal, in short, are that the respondents herein as writ petitioners filed writ petition being Writ Petition No.3630 of 1999 before the High Court Division for release/de-requisition of unused land of 6.24 acres of Mouza Foidabad of Cadastral Survey (in short C.C.) Plot Nos.694, 696, 1071, 802, 951, 954, 824, 826, 950, 952 and 1070 and direction for payment of compensation of used land measuring 9.91 acres of Mouza Foidabad of C.S. Plot Nos.788, 965, 877, 948, 811, 806, 867, 870, 880, 811, 829, 835, 827, 839, 840, 841, 844, 845, 847, 852, 862, 863, 864, 879, 884, 842, 843, 847, 848, 861, 863, 879, 881, 807, and 778 which was requisitioned in L.A. Case No.8/64 65 and in L.A. Case No.66/57-58 for development of Uttara Model Town stating, inter alia, that they are the heirs of the C.S. recorded tenant Probhat Ali and Darbesh Ali who were the owners of the total land measuring an area of 16.15 acres of land in Foidabad Mouza within the District Dhaka, and became the owners of the said land by inheritance, purchase and also by way of amicable partition. The writ-respondent Nos.5 and 6 requisitioned the huge area including the above lands in L.A. Case No.66/1957-58 and L.A. Case No.8/64-65 of Dhaka Collectorate under section 93A of the Town Improvement Act, 1952 (E.P. Act No. XIII of 1953) for creating a residential area named Uttara Model Town. Further case of the writ-petitioners is that statutory notices were not served upon the predecessor of the writ-petitioners or upon the writ petitioners, no compensation was paid to the predecessor of the writ petitioners or to the writ petitioners and more-so, the lands covered by the aforesaid plots were not published in the Gazette. The power of attorney holder of the writ petitioners sent a letter on 26.08.1999 to the Manager (Administration) Bangladesh Forms and Publications office, Tejgaon, Dhaka asking him to know whether those plots were published in the Gazette or not, the said Manager replied on 06.09.1999 that the said plots were not published in the Gazette. The requiring body i.e., writ-respondent No.3 took possession of the land of L.A. Case except the plot Nos.694, 696, 1071, 802, 951, 955, 824, 826, 950, 952 and 1070, the writ petitioners are in possession thereof by erecting shops since the time of their predecessors. The writ respondent No.3 neither took possession of the lands in question nor the same was developed for the purpose of establishing of Uttara Model Town for which the lands were acquired. It was alleged in the writ petition that all of a sudden on 7.3.1999 the Duty Officer of Uttara Police Station served a notice upon the writ petitioners and to their power of attorney holder Md. Mukarram Hossain under section 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to remove their shops and houses from the scheduled land. Thereafter, on receipt of the said notice on 18.03.1999, a legal notice was served upon the writ-respondent No.3 stating that the scheduled land were not legally requisitioned, as such, appropriate action is required to be taken against the aforesaid L.A. Cases. It was further alleged that thereafter, the power of attorney holder Md. Mukarram Hossain on behalf of all the writ petitioners on 01-07-1999 filed two applications before the writ-respondent No.5 praying for compensation money for the lands which was used and for lease of the lands which was in possession of the writ petitioners and on inquiry Md. Mukarram Hossain, the power of attorney holder of the writ petitioners came to know that a meeting of the Ministry of Land, section 10, Government of Bangladesh, was held on 2.6.1988 and it is revealed from the serial Nos. 13 and 31 of the proceedings of the said meeting, the Government has decided that the land must be used within 3 (three) years from the 'date of acquisition and further decided that 3 katha of plot will be allotted to the affected family but about 11 years have been elapsed without executing the said resolution. The said Mukarram Hossain also inquired into the office of writ-respondent No.3 and found that the RAJUK has decided to sale in auction the lands in question to the highest bidder after developing the said lands as commercial plots, thus, C.S. recorded tenant moved Writ Petition No.7019 of 1997 before the High Court Division where the RAJUK filed an affidavit-in-opposition stating that they will sell those lands after developing the lands. The alleged acquisition took place on 23.09.1965 but land in questions have not been utilized more than 35 years, as such, it is presumed that the requiring body is not in need of the said unutilized land for the purpose of which it was acquisitioned, as such, it is liable to be derequisitioned. The aforesaid L.A. Case is ultra vires of the provision of section 93(A)(4)(h) of the Town Improvement Act, 1953. The writ petitioners further case is that no compensation money has ever been paid to the writ-petitioners or to their predecessor-ininterest tall today, as such, the L.A. case is liable to be declared as without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. The writ petitioner further stated that on 30.10.1984, the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms expressed their views that the lands which were purportedly acquired but not used by the requiring body till today should be given back to the owners and the same cannot be kept unused for indefinite period. On the basis of the aforesaid decision of the Government a circular was issued on 02.05.1986 by the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms where it was categorically stated that the purported acquired lands, the possession of which has not been taken by the requiring body should be returned to the owners and according to the aforesaid circular, the Government already returned several hundred unused lands to the previous owners. The writ petitioners further stated that after acquiring the property from the poor people, the RAJUK has sold some of those lands to their employees who developed the same as commercial area and made their fortune. Therefore, the writ petitioners being aggrieved by the aforesaid actions of the writ-respondents and finding no other alternative efficacious remedy moved the above mentioned writ petition before the High Court Division and obtained the Rule Nisi. 

3. The writ respondents contested the Rule Nisi by filing affidavit-in-opposition stating that the lands in question were lawfully acquired vide in L.A. Case No. 13149-50 and 8/64-65 by the writ-respondent No.5 following the statutory procedures and possession of the said land was handed over to the requiring body, the then D.I.T. at present RAJUK on 3 different dates i.e. 19.01.1966, 30.11.1967 and 09.05.1968. It is further explained that as per the then prevailing market value of compensation was awarded to the then owners of the land in question showing award of compensation and receipt of compensation by the then owners of the s id land. It is also described that the writ respondents took possession of C.S. Plot Nos. 694, 696, 1071, 802, 951, 955, 824, 826, 950, 952 and 1070 in 1966 along with other land lawfully acquired for the purpose of developing and setting up the Uttara Model Town. The RAJUK, the requiring body started the process of developing the Uttara Model Town and thereby divided the above C.S. Plots into different section under a layout plan of the Uttara Model Town. The RAJUK further stated in their affidavit-in-opposition that some of the C.S. recorded tenant has filed writ petition before the High Court Division and the same was discharged. That it has been further stated that the Appellate Division in the decision decided that mere non use of the acquired land for the purported purpose for which it was acquired will not give any right to its previous owner to get return of the same and it was also decided in some other cases also. That it is further stated that inspite of the repeal of sections 93A and 93B of the said Act provision of section 12 of 1982 Ordinance will not be applied in respect of the requisition of the land in question in view of the provisions of section 6 of the General Clauses Act. 

4. A Division Bench of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties disposed the Rule Nisi by the impugned judgment and order dated 27.06.2001. 

5. Feeling aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order dated 27.06.2001 of the High Court Division, the Government of Bangladesh and others as petitioners herein preferred the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1206 of 2002 before this Division and obtained leave, which, gave rise to the instant appeal. 

6. Mr. Mohammad Shaiful Alam, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that the High Court Division acted beyond its jurisdiction in holding that admittedly the writ-petitioners are poor people that they are also entitled to get alternative plots on proving their prima-facie title and ownership in the lands in question, despite the fact that it is for the requiring body to decide as to whether the writ-petitioners are entitled to get alter-native plots or not and, hence, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside by this Hon'ble Court and the appeal may kindly be allowed. He further submits that the lands in question having been acquired in L.A. Case No.13/49-50 and 8/64-65 by the Government following the statutory proceedings and possession of the lands having been handed over to the requiring body, the High Curt Division erred in law in making directions and not discharging the rule as being not maintainable and, as such, the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside and the appeal may kindly be allowed. He next submits that the requiring body (RAJUK) having started process of developing the lands and making different lands and making different plots under layout plan of Uttara Model Town for allotment, but the High Court Division erred in law in not discharging rule and, as such, the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside and the instant appeal may kindly be allowed. He finally submits that in view of Provisions of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, the provisions of Section 12 of 1982 Ordinance not being applicable in this case inspite of repeal of Section 93A and 93B of the Town Improvement Act, but the High Court Division erred in law in making the direction in disposing the rule Nisi and, as such, the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside and the instant appeal may kindly be allowed. 

7. No one appears on behalf of the respondents. 

8. We have heard the learned Assistant Attorney General for the appellants. Perused the impugned judgment of the High Court Division and other connected materials on record. 

9. Leave was granted to examine the following submission of the learned Deputy Attorney General for the appellants as to that: 
"The High Court Division acted beyond its jurisdiction in holding that admittedly the writ-petitioners are poor people that they are also entitled to get alternative plots on proving their prima-facie title and ownership in the lands in question, despite the fact that it is for the requiring body to decide as to whether the writ-petitioners are entitled to get alternative plots or not hence the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside by this Hon'ble Court." 

10. At this juncture, let us weigh up the materials on record as to whether judgment and order of High Court Division is justified or erred which calls for interference by this Division. 

11. The cardinal points raised by the respondents-writ petitioners for seeking remedies are that the acquiring authority did not use the acquired land for years and there was a ministerial Communication for releasing the land so acquired. In the case of Al-Haj Abul Basher being dead his heirs (a) Hosne Ara Begum and others vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 1997 17 BLD (AD) 321 this Division observed in the matters "non-use of the: land for years" and "Ministerial Communications" as to that: 
"Mere non-use of the land for years will not give any right to the petitioners. We also find that after completing all necessary formalities the land had already been handed over to the requiring body namely, CDA. Since no legal or vested right has accrued in favour of the petitioners by mere Inter Ministerial Communications the petitioners cannot have any legal right to ask for return of the land. Further the Inter Ministerial Communications are merely internal policy decisions and guidelines for the various departments of the Government and the same is not a declared policy decision of the Government. Hence, no abuse of discretion or arbitrariness or unfair treatment can be attributed to the executive government, as there is also no lawful obligation on the part of the Government to act on intend circulars and decisions so far as it relates to the petitioners. Respondent No. 1 has acted lawfully within the scheme of Emergency Requisition: of Property Act, 1948 and the same cannot be said to be arbitrary, unfair and illegal.” 

12. The same issue of releasing the unutilized land from requisition has also been dealt with by this Division in the case of Badal Rani Misra alias Badal Rani Goswami and others Vs. Bangladesh and others, reported in 27 DLR(AD) 65 wherein this Decision observed that: 
"The question relating to the release of requisitioned land falls within the administrative function of the requisitioning authority And if the said authority considered it necessary to seek approval of the Government before passing an order of release of the same, it does not appear how that discretion called for interference by the High Court Division and how the High Court Division could pass an order of release under the Requisition of Property Act.”  

13. In the case of Government of Bangladesh and others =Versus= Dewan Fakhrul Alam and others reported in 27 BLT (AD) (2019) 144, this Division was held that- "We have gone through the provisions of sub section 7 of Section 5 of the Requisition of Property Act which deal with the publication of the gazette and not release from the requisition of any property and withdrawal from the acquisition. However, we do not find any such provisions in the law that if any land after payment of compensation is remained unused that would be the basis to asking for release of the same from acquisition, even if, publication of the gazette notification has not yet done under sub section 7 of Section 5 of the Requisition of Property Act. Therefore, the contentions advanced by Mr. Nazrul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Senior Counsel referring the provision of section 5(7) of the Requisition of the Property Act pointed that since the final gazette notification has not yet been published, therefore, the aforesaid land in question has not been finally acquired and no title has vest with the Government. Therefore, according to Section 8 of the Act, the property in question can be released by the Government are completely devoid of legal propositions.” 

14. The same view placed in the case of Government of Bangladesh and others =Versus= Dewan Fakhrul Alam and others reported in 27 BLT (AD) (2019) 144, this Division was further held that- 
"Our considered views are that the land in question cannot be released from the acquisition because as per Section 5(6) of the Requisition of Property Act compensation has already been paid to the owner. So, there is no scope to withdraw the proposal of the acquisition and return back the land to the person from whom the same has been acquired although the final gazette has not yet been published." 

15. Allotting alternative plots and deciding whether the respondents-writ petitioners a destitute and in meager economic condition is policy decision of the requiring body or matter of social safety network of the government, not a matter to be judicially decided reviemed. As such to allot plots to the original owner of the acquired land is beyond the jurisdiction of the courts. 

16. Moreover, as per section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 "Abatement or revocation of acquisition proceedings" under section 12 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 is not applicable in spite of repeal of section 93A and 93B. Section 6 of the said Act is as such: 
"Effect of repeal 
6. Where this Act, or any 1 [Act of Parliament] or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act, repeals any enactment hitherto made or hereafter to be made, then, unless a different intention appears, the repeal shall not- 
(a)revive anything not in force or existing at the time at which the repeal takes effect; or 
(b) affect the previous operation of any enactment so repealed or anything duly done or suffered thereunder; 

17. Accordingly, we find merit in submissions of the learned Assistant Attorney General for the appellants. 

18. Hence, this appeal is allowed without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside. 

End.

full_judgment:
This is an application for addition of party.
2. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the applicant, submits that the applicant-company is a subsidiary of Hungama Digital Media Entertainment Private Limited which is a company incorporated in India and the applicant-company represents its parent company in Bangladesh.
3. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam further submits that the parent company, that is to say, Hungama Digital Media Entertainment Private Limited is the largest Digital Media Company in South Asia and launched India's first and largest on-demand digital entertainment storefront which has over two and a half million pieces of content across genres and languages in the form of music tracks, movies, music videos and dialogue mobile contents such as ringtones and wallpapers.
4. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam next submits that the applicant-company has been engaged in importing contents such as Hindi film songs and Hindi songs of its parent company and distributing the same to different entities including mobile telecommunication service-providers in Bangladesh and the applicant-company had been helping the consumers of this country to relish and use the contents of its parent company through mobile telecommunication service-providers.
5. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam further submits that since the applicant-company has been importing the said contents in Bangladesh and as the interim order dated 9-7-2015 passed in the Writ Petition has been greatly affecting the business of the applicant-company, it is necessary to implead the same as a respondent in the instant Writ Petition.
6. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam also submits that although it has been stated in Article 54(c) of the Articles of Association of the applicant-company that the Managing Director, subject to the approval of the Board of Directors, is expressly authorized to exercise the powers to institute, conduct, defend, compound or abandon any legal proceeding by or against the Company or its officers or otherwise concerning the affairs of the Company and also to compound and allow of demands by or against the Company; but this Article 54(c) has not in any way restricted the power of the Board of Directors to authorize any non-employee to act for and on behalf of the company in any proceeding in a, Court of law and for all practical purposes, the Board of Directors is the supreme authority of the company and its Managing Director is always subject to the control and supervision of the Board of Directors and given this scenario, the Board of Directors of the applicant-company is competent enough to authorize Md Iqbal Hossain, Managing Partner of Safe FI to act for and on behalf of the applicant-company in this proceeding before this Court.
7. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam also submits that the Board of Directors of the applicant-company gave a letter of authorization in favour of Md Iqbal Hossain on 7-10-2016 pursuant to a resolution of the Board of Directors dated 7-10-2016 authorizing him to act for and on behalf of the applicant-company in this proceeding; but Md Iqbal Hossain. Managing Partner of Safe Fl, signed the power on behalf of Safe FI and not on behalf of the applicant-company and this technical mistake stands cured by the subsequent resolution of the Board of Directors and the letter of authorization as evidenced by Annexure-'2' series to the Supplementary Affidavit dated 10-7-2017 filed on behalf of the applicant-company.
8. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam lastly submits that although Md Iqbal Hossain is not an officer or employee of the applicant-company; but even then, he has been legally authorized by the Board of Directors of the applicant-company to represent the company in this proceeding before this Court. In support of this submission, Mr Tanjib-ul Alam has drawn our attention to the decision dated 26-4-2012 in the case of Arun Kumar Singhania vs State of MP and others passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh and the decision dated 17-11-2008 in the case of National Small Industries Corporation Ltd. vs State (NCT of Delhi) and others passed by the Supreme Court of India which were downloaded from the website Manupatra.
9. Per contra, Mr Sheikh Fazle Noor Taposh, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner-opposite-parties, submits that Md Iqbal Hossain, Managing Partner of Safe FI, cannot represent the applicant-company in view of the fact that admittedly he is neither an officer nor a director nor an employee of the applicant-company and in that view of the matter, Md Iqbal Hossain cannot be authorized by the Board of Directors to represent the company in this proceeding before this Court.
10. Mr Sheikh Fazle Noor Taposh further submits that Order 29, rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure contemplates that in suits by or against a corporation, any pleading may be signed and verified on behalf of the corporation by the secretary or by any director or other principal officer of the corporation who is able to depose to the facts of the case and as Md Iqbal Hossain is not an employee or any officer or any director of the applicant-company, he is not able to depose to the facts of the case as a matter of course and in this perspective, the application for addition of party is liable to be rejected.
11. Mr Sheikh Fazle Noor Taposh next submits that unless Article 54 of the Articles of Association of the applicant-company is amended, Md Iqbal, a non-employee of the applicant-company, cannot be authorized by any resolution of the Board of Directors to represent the company in this case.
12. Mr Sheikh Fazle Noor Taposh also submits by referring to the decision in the case of Alauddin Masum vs Mosammat Aleya Begum and others reported in 23 BLT (AD) 1 = 67 DLR (AD) 136 that a necessary party is one without whom no order can be effectively made and a proper party is one whose presence is necessary for complete or final decision of the question involved in the matter and the Court is to determine whether the presence of the applicant-company is necessary for the disposal of the Rule.
13. We have heard submissions of the learned Advocate Mr Tanjib-ul Alam and the counter-submissions of the learned Advocate Mr Sheikh Fazle Noor Taposh and perused the application and the Affidavit-in-Opposition filed there against and other relevant documents and Annexures annexed thereto.
14. Be that as it may, on 9-7-2015, this Court issued a Rule Nisi calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the act of allowing the respondent Nos. 6-11 to use Hindi film songs, Hindi songs or Indian Bengali film songs or sub-continental film songs as ringtones or welcome tunes or any other value-added services for mobile phones should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect being violative of section 26(49) of the Import Policy Order, 2012-2014 and why the respondent Nos. 1-5 should not be directed to restrain the respondent Nos. 6-11 from using Hindi film songs, Hindi songs or Indian Bengali film songs or sub-continental film songs as ringtones or welcome tunes or any other value-added services for mobile phones and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.
15. Admittedly the applicant-company is a subsidiary of Hungama Digital Media Entertainment Private Limited which is a company. incorporated in India. In other words, the applicant-company represents its parent company in Bangladesh. It transpires from the averments made in the application for addition of party that the applicant-company has been engaged in importing contents such as Hindi film songs and Hindi songs of its parent company and distributing the same to different entities including mobile telecommunication service-providers in Bangladesh. So the operation of the applicant-company being a subsidiary of the Indian company in Bangladesh is ex-facie clear.
16. Precisely speaking, we are to see as to whether the presence of the applicant-company is necessary for proper and effectual adjudication of the Rule. In this connection, Mr Sheikh Fazle Noor Taposh has taken an initial objection to the competency of the applicant-company to file the instant application for addition of party. According to him, Md Iqbal Hossain, Managing Partner of Safe FL, cannot represent the applicant-company inasmuch as indisputably he is neither any employee nor any director nor any officer of the applicant-company and that being so, Md Iqbal Hossain cannot represent the applicant-company in this proceeding before this Court. It is also the contention of Mr Sheikh Fazle Noor Taposh that according to Article 54(c) of the Articles of Association of the applicant-company, it is only the Managing Director of the company who is authorized to institute, conduct, defend, compound or abandon any legal proceeding by or against the company or its officers or otherwise concerning the affairs of the company and also to compound and allow of demands by or against the company subject to the approval of the Board of Directors. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam concedes to the fact that as per Article 54 of the Articles of Association of the applicant-company, the Managing Director of the company has been authorized in that regard subject to the approval of the Board of Directors. However, the Board of Directors of a company is its supreme authority and the Managing Director is always subject to the control and supervision of the Board of Directors. Even the Board of Directors may pass any resolution or directive which is not specifically contemplated by the Articles of Association in the interest of the company, if the situation so demands. Although any non-employee of the applicant-company has not been specifically mentioned in Article 54 of the Articles of Association for authorization to represent the company in any legal proceeding; yet none the less, the Board of Directors, being the supreme authority of the company, has the right to authorize any non-employee of the company to represent it in any legal proceeding before any Court of law. What we are driving at boils down to this: Article 54 of the Articles of Association of the applicant-company has not in any way derogated from the authority of the Board of Directors to authorize Md Iqbal Hossain, Managing Partner of Safe Fl, to represent the applicant-company in this proceeding.
17. In the case of National Small Industries Corporation Ltd. vs State (NCT of Delhi) and others which was decided on 17-11-2008 by the Supreme Court of India, it was spelt out:
"If the payee is a company, necessarily the complaint should be filed in the name of the company. Section 142 of the NI Act does not specify who should represent the company, if a company is the complainant. A company can be represented by an employee or even by a non-employee authorized and empowered to represent the company either by a resolution or by a power of attorney."
18. In the rase of Arun Kumar Singhania vs State of MP and others which was decided by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh on 26-4-2012, it was observed:
"Indisputably, in the complaint as well as in the civil suit filed by the petitioner Arun Singhania, AK Agrawal has been impleaded as one of the persons in-charge of and responsible for conduct of business of the Company. Although, he claims that necessary authorization was given to him by way of resolutions dated 19-4-2010 and 10-2-2011 yet, it is well-settled that a company can be represented by an employee or even by a non-employee authorized and empowered to represent the company either by a resolution or by a power-of-attorney. Moreover, merely because the complaint is signed and presented by a person, who is neither an authorized agent nor a person empowered under the Articles of Association or by any resolution of the Board to do so, the same is no ground to quash the complaint since the defect is curable."
19. It is an admitted fact that Md Iqbal Hossain, Managing Partner of Safe FI, executed a power in this case on 23-2-2017. It is further admitted that on or before that date (23-2-2017), there was no Board resolution or any authorization of Md Iqbal Hossain by the Board to represent the applicant-company in this proceeding before this Court. In other words, the resolution of the Board of Directors of the applicant-company and the authorization in favour of Md Iqbal Hossain are subsequent in point of time. At tile time of execution of the power by Md Iqbal Hossain, he was, as we see him, was not competent to represent the applicant-company in this case; but after passing of the subsequent resolution by the Board of Directors and rendition of the authorization in favour of Md Iqbal Hossain the initial defect in his competency to represent the company was cured and the action of Md lqbal Hossain in executing the power was ratified as evidenced by Annexure-'2' series to the Supplementary Affidavit dated 10-7-2017 filed on behalf of the applicant-company.
<u>20. It is true that as per Order 29, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, in suits by or against a corporation, any pleading may be signed and verified on behalf of the corporation by the secretary or by any director or other principal officer of the corporation who is able to depose to the facts of the case. In this respect, it may be pointed out that the scope and purpose of a Writ Petition are manifestly different from a civil suit. The principles relating to addition of parties in a civil suit are not protanto applicable to a Writ Petition. This view finds support from the decision in the case of Moudud Ahmed vs Anwar Hossain Khan, Advocate and others reported in 1995 BLD (AD) 12. So we are led to hold that the principles relating to addition of party in a civil suit are not wholly applicable to the present proceeding of the Writ Petition. We have already found that even a non-employee can represent any company, if he is duly authorized by the Board of Directors of that company. Moreover, it is in the affidavit sworn by Md Iqbal Hossain that he is acquainted with the facts of the case. In such a situation, the invocation of Order 29, rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure will not be of any avail to Mr Sheikh Fazle Noor Taposh.</u>
<u>21. Undeniably the applicant-company is a subsidiary of Hungama Digital Media Entertainment Private Limited which is incorporated in India. In Bangladesh, the applicant-company is operating its business on behalf of the parent company Hungama Digital Media Entertainment Private Limited. If, for the sake of argument, the Rule is heard and made absolute on merit in the absence of the applicant-company, it will definitely be highly prejudiced. In the facts and circumstances of the case and in the premises made above, we find that the applicant-company is vitally interested in the subject matter of the Rule and that being so, the presence of the applicant is necessary for proper and effectual adjudication of the Rule. Accordingly, the application is allowed.</u>
22. Let the applicant, namely, Hungama Bangladesh Private Limited represented by its authorized representative Md lqbal Hossain, Managing partner, Safe FI, 3rd Floor, House 39, Road 126, Gulshan South Avenue, Dhaka- 1212 be impleaded as respondent No. 12 to the Writ Petition.
Office is directed to amend the cause-title of the Writ Petition and the register accordingly.
End.

Nawroz Md Rasel Chowdhury, DAG and MMG Sarwar (Payel), Masud Rana Mohammad Hafiz and Tamanna Ferdous, AAGs—For the Respondent No.2.
